THE NIPIGON IRON RANGE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: That the petition of Hamilton Cassels and others, presented this day, praying to be permitted to lay before t,he House their petition for an Act of incorporation under the name of Nipigon Iron Range Railway Company, notwithstanding the expiration of the time for presenting petitions for private Bills, be now read and received, and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders.

maintopic: THE NIPIGON IRON RANGE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I merely want to say in regard to this that the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said that last session he intended to stop the practice of extending the time for the introduction of Bills after the time had passed. I simply draw his attention to it now so that it will not be continued too far, because it is one of the means by which our sessions are often lengthened, and as every one must have reasonable notice when a Bill is introduced, giving notice so late in the session and then bringing Bills in after the time has expired for receiving Bills or petitions is an improper thing and it should be discontinued.

maintopic: THE NIPIGON IRON RANGE RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule). Last session we shortened the time of these extensions which had occurred time after time, but if the House is warned in advance that this final extension will be finally final it will act accordingly and I hope we will not be called upon to extend it later on.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: That the petition of Philip Demers and others, presented this day, praying for leave to present the petition of James Sinclair Mc-Dougall, for an Act to authorize the committee of patents to receive a partial fee and revive certain letters patent of invention, notwithstanding the expiration of the time for receiving petitions for private Bills, be now' read and received and referred to the Select Standing Committee on Standing Orders.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: Despite the fact that the right hon. Prime Minister has said that this has been made finally final, it is becoming a bad habit.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: The time limit ought to expire in regard to a Bill of that kind.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: The time limit must be extended to all or none.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have already called the attention of the House to the fact that by a recent decision of the Supreme Court in the matter of patents a great many patents have lapsed. I have seen on the Order Paper for a long time a Bill proposed to be introduced by the hon. Minister of Agricul-true (Hon. Mr. Fisher). I think that Bill, if it were carried, would remedy the evils which are complained of in the present instance. I would urge upon the government the necessity of pressing this Bill, if it is to be pressed, as soon as possible, so that it will be passed this session. If it is not passed this session, I may tell the government, what probably the government know already, that a vast injustice will be done to a great many owners of patents.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: In answer to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) I may say that I think he is mistaken in supposing that these private Bills are of the same nature as the government Bill referred to. I think these Bills would be necessary any way, but the Bill of which notice has been given in the name of the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Hon. Mr. Fisher) will be brought forward at an early day. The hon. minister is on his way home and we would prefer that he should deal with the subject himself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: I would take the liberty of calling the attention of the government to a point that should be remedied in any Bill which is introduced. A person applies for a patent and before it issues from the department one of his workmen leaves his employment, gives away the secret to another firm that begins to manufacture and under the law no injunction can be obtained restraining this firm from using this patent and there are no means of bringing cases of that kind to an issue.

maintopic: MR. JAMES SINCLAIR McDOUGALL-REVIYAL OF PATENT.
speechtext: The remedy would be by an amendment to the regulations of the department providing means by which an issue of that kind might be brought forward more quickly than by the present regulation, which allows two years. The matter is now engaging the attention of the department.
Motion agreed to.

Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I wish to bring before the House a matter which I spoke of last night before the adjournment. At the outset 1 wish to say that the remarks I intend to make are not at all dictated by any motives of personal hostility towards Lord Duudonald. I have not the advantage or the pleasure of knowing the gentleman; and, anyhow, I would consider it to be unworthy of ny position as a member of this House to make a personal attack upon any official of this government. If my remarks had reference only to the personal opinions of Lord Dundonald, as an official of the government, my attack would naturally have to be directed against the responsible head of the Militia Department, that is, the hon. Minister of Militia (Sir Frederick W. Borden); but some of the utterances of Lord Dundonald should, I think, bring to the mind of the House the general subject of the relations that should exist between the responsible head of the Militia Department and the officers sent by the British government to take the position of commander of our militia. This is not a new matter. It has been a source of difficulty in the past between nearly all Ministers of Militia and officers commanding our militia; so that I say-and this is the point I wish to make to-day-that the weakness in our system does not come from the choice of the man, but comes from the system itself, and that it should be remedied as soon as possible.
On the 23rd of April last, at a large banquet which was held in the city of Hamilton in honour of St. George's day, Lord Mr. SPEAKER
Dundonald made a lengthy and eloqueut speech.
What paper are you quoting from ?

I am quoting from the Hamilton ' Times ' of April 24. In the speech he spoke at length about the reorganization of the militia in Canada, and I quote two paragraphs :
It was too late to organize when the storm-cloud had burst, organization must be done before. The more civilian the force, the more perfect should be the organization. What he wanted in Canada, was that when he touched a button in his central office that every regiment in the land could be called out lit for service. Was this the case now ? he asked. (No ! no ! from several voices)	
The militia, he was afraid, had had as their diet promises for a long time, instead of food, praise exuberant, instead of wine. What was wanted, was a little of that thirteen millions of dollars. He did not wish to create that bugbear-the spirit of militarism, but he did want to see an efficient force in Canada-a force efficient in all its departments, and having every facility for imparting every information to the officers to enable them to properly command their men. This was not militarism, it was common sense.
To these words of the officer, taken by themselves, I make no objection; but the point which I want to make, and which I will make still more strongly from some further utterances of Lord Dundonald, is that he is not the proper person to declare what should be the military policy of Canada. The Minister of Militia is the proper authority to give an opinion as to what reforms should be made in the militia of Canada, because he is the man whom the people and the parliament of Canada have a right to criticise and vote against if his policy does not suit them.
On the previous day, the 22nd of April, Lord Dundonald was passing through Toronto, where he gave an interview which I find in the Ottawa ' Citizen ' of April the 23rd. In that interview he said :
Some people may endeavour to discourage what they deem militarism, but it can be understood how futile the strength of the defensive force of Canada would be without it. That is simply what I shall endeavour to bring about in the Canadian militia, organization on reasonable and sensible lines. I shall be in Toronto in a short time, and I shall have an opportunity of stating publicly my opinions re-ga.rding the organization of the volunteer forces and I am sure they will meet with the approval of those who understand the governing of Canada, her position in the empire, and her standing in the world.
Here there was a slight difference. In the speech at the banquet Lord Dundonald said that far from his mind was the idea of favouring the spirit of militarism; but in the interview at Toronto he said that the only way of improving our militia was by fostering that spirit. To this declaration I am glad to say we have a strong and fore-

ible answer from the lion. Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), who, speaking at the same banquet at Hamilton, made a speech against the spirit of militarism. I have already had occasion to express to that lion, gentleman my opinion of that speech, and here X have pleasure in saying that it is one of the most promising declarations we have had from a responsible member of the government since the conference in London. I will quote one paragraph from that speech :
Militarism is the enemy of true liberty, and its adoption in Canada would go to weaken, if not destroy, the bond of union now so firmly and happily uniting us with the great mother of nations.
It is Canada's ambition to follow all that is glorious in the annals of Great Britain. Canadian citizenship Is now being extended to vast numbers of people, who, weary of old-world burdens, disappointments or oppressions, come here to breathe the air of free Canada, to share with us in her bounteous gifts and assist us in building up in this western world a Greater Britain, suggesting the thought that the centre of empire may yet be in British North America (cheers). But be that as it may, Canada's task awaits her.
Ever guided by the torch of liberty, instead of destroying with the sword, let her aim be to acquire industrial dominion over her fertile lands, her productive waters, her mines, her forests, to drive away the solitude of her vast unoccupied areas with the cheerful music of human voices and hum of productive machinery; to awaken her dormant wealth, lying everywhere easily within man's grasp ; to extend her commerce to the uttermost corners of the earth, and to make the name of Canada everywhere stand for freedom and progress.
I need not say, Sir, that this Is a national programme to which every member of this House should be happy to assent.
On the 1st of April last the Dominion Rifle Association met at Ottawa. Lord Dundon-ald was present, and here Is a quotation from his speech on that occasion, which I take from the ' Citizen ' of the 2nd of April : Though I have recommended certain steps which I think are necessary for the militia, I wish here emphatically to deny a falsehood current in certain papers, namely, that I was much annoyed that $12,000,.000 was not provided in this year's estimates for the militia for capital expenditure. If $12,000,000 were provided this moment I could not with the moderate proposals I made recommend its expenditure with advantage within a year. Such expenditure might well be spread over two or three years so that organization in men and their efficiency could go hand in hand with the provision of material.
The gentleman leaves us the hope that we may have the chance of getting our share of the surplus of 513,000,000 for the development of trade and industry in Canada, but he warns us that his intention Is to swallow it up in three years instead of one year. I know very well that this is not the policy of the government. The hon. Minister of Militia (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) has expressed clearly, within the last six months, on several 76
occasions, what is the policy of the government with regard to militia matters. In only one of those speeches was there perhaps a tendency expressed similar to that stated by Lord Dundonald, but when I brought that speech to the attention of the hon. minister he said emphatically that the report was incorrect. We have further the strong expression of opinion given by the hon. Postmaster General, which I have already quoted. The point I want to make is this, that on militia matters, or any matters whatever connected with the expenditure of the people's money, it is not proper that we should have on one side a programme laid down by one of the irresponsible officials of one of the departments and another programme on the other side laid down by the responsible head of that department. Suppose the Minister of Public Works were to declare at a banquet that he was in favour of deepening the Ottawa river, or building the Georgian Bay canal, and that while he did not want the
513,000,000 surplus of this year spent for that purpose, he would spread the expenditure over three or four years ; and then suppose we had the minister responsible for that department stating at another banquet that it was not the intention of the government to do either of these works would not any member of this House say that such a state of affairs should not be encouraged ? Would not likewise any member of this House, whatever may be his opinions on militia matters and the relations that should exist between this country and the old country with regard to military organization, and who knows anything about responsible government, say that we should not tolerate any irresponsible official declaring publicly for a policy which the government disavows?
An liou. MEMBER. It is funny that all those quotations are from speeches made at banquets.

Yes, and the funniest thing is that the most reasonable of those quotations, which I have given, are from speeches that were made at banquets. The most reasonable quotation was from a speech made by the hon. Postmaster General at a banquet. The other quotation was from an interview given to the reporter of a newspaper, and the third was from a speech made in the city of Ottawa at the meeting of the Dominion Rifle Association. If the views expressed by Lord Dundonald do not represent the policy of the government- and we have the best of evidence that they do not-then we are in the presence of a struggle between an irresponsible official of the government and the responsible head of the department. Certainly that condition of things cannot be allowed to continuer As I have said, I am not attacking Lord Dundonald personally. But we have had from the beginning to the end, the same conflict



between every British commander of our militia and every Minister of Militia, and no doubt the cause is to be found in the fact that our law provides that the officer commanding our militia shall be sent here by the British government. The result is obvious. The gentleman who leaves the other side to take command of our militia has no intention of becoming one of our own, and does not come here to take his responsibility as a Canadian officer. He comes here to introduce into the military organization of Canada such reforms as may be pointed out by the head of the War Office in the mother country. Not being a military man, I shall not attempt to discuss the value, from a military point of view, of Lord Dundonald's merits ; but what I say is that there should be a distinct understanding between this government and the government of the old country that in military, as well as in other matters, this is a self-governing country and that any military regulations and laws which may commend Oiemselves to our approval we will adopt of our own free will at the suggestion of the responsible head of the department and not at the suggestion of an officer who becomes, the moment he lands, a paid official of this government, and lias consequently no right to direct our policy. This is not merely a personal opinion I am expressing. Difference of views between the officer commanding the militia and the responsible head of the Militia Department is considered in England as a struggle between the imperial and the Canadian authorities. As evidence of this let me quote from the London ' Morning Post ' of the 30th of April last, which has a long article on the position of Canada from a military point of view. In that article, after some words about the progress of military spirit in Canada, I find this paragraph :-
But it does not go nearly far enough, and we should not he surprised if the report that the Earl of Dundonald is dissatisfied with the government's response to his request for more men, better guns, and a more thorough organization turned out to be substantially correct. Nor is it altogether certain that Lord Dundonald has succeeded in preventing the use of military appointments as rewards for services to a ruling political party.
We have here one of the leaders of public opinion in the capital of the empire discussing the matter as a struggle between the officer commanding and the Canadian Minister of Militia. If this opinion exists in the old country, it should be dissipated as rapidly as possible, not only from our point of view but from the imperial point of view ; because so long as the leading men in England are not perfectly convinced that whatever may be the policy of Canada with regard to military or other matters, that policy will manifest itself in laws and regulations adopted by our Canadian parliament, and not according to the dictates of any irresponsible officer, we are likely to see no Mr. BOURASSA.
end to this continual friction between those officers sent out by the British government to command our militia and the Canadian government.
I do not think that I need add very much to what I have said. I have not brought this question up from a military point of view but as a layman. Judging, however, by what I have read on the subject in the newspapers in England, particularly the military and naval newspapers, I think that while on many matters perhaps British officers have more experience than ours, in some matters they have an experience that rather unfits them for the direction of the military organization of this country. No body of officers of this country, for example, would stand being flogged for not having had proper uniforms on when going to the barber shop in the morning. That is an extreme idea of military discipline which would not be tolerated in this country. As regards the vote for military expenditure by this parliament, no doubt, whatever may be our individual opinion on the amount of money which should be expended, there is no division of opinion in this parliament as to the authority which should decide on that expenditure and how the money should be expended. Therefore we should on this occasion, as we did in the case of General Hutton, call for an explanation from the government, so that the lines may be drawn clearly ae regards the real position of the officer commanding our militia and the relations that exist between him and the responsible head of the Militia Department.

I think it would be very much out of place on this occasion to enter into any discussion of any proposal with reference to military expenditure which may be under the consideration of the government, although my hon. friend has tempted us perhaps to follow in that direction. I think, however, that the question he has brought up is one to which the House may very profitably give a few moments consideration. I do not, I may say at the outset agree with my hon. friend in his criticism of the utterances of the present officer commanding. I have failed to discover in the quotations which he has read anything which the most exacting member of the government or member of parliament could take exception to. Nor do I think, from my knowledge of the intentions of the present general that he intended to say anything of an improper character, or that he intended to assume powers which did not properly belong to him. To say, for instance, that it is too late when the storm has passed-to prepare for a storm-we cannot take much exception to that. To say that he desires to have every battalion in Canada, so far as we have battalions, in a state of efficiency is not a thing that one could take exception to. Not only that, but I may say that I endorse

absolutely the desire expressed by the General that, so far as we have a militia in this country, it shall be an effective militia. Nor do I quarrel very much with the statement which the General appears to have made that the militia of Canada has had promises too long and performances for too short a time. I would agree with him in that; I would like to see more performance. But I agree with my hon. friend when he leaves the particular case under consideration and traverses the broader field. I agree with him entirely when he says that the general officer commanding the troops in this country is a servant of the people of Canada, and an official of the government of Canada. I think there has been, in the past, some misapprehension in this matter in the minds of gentlemen who come to this country to occupy the prominent position of the general officer commanding the Canadian militia. Some three years ago, it became the duty of the First Minister to state very distinctly the views of the government with reference to this matter. And I shall take occasion before I sit down to read the words to which the Prime Minister gave utterances at that time. But, before doing so, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I have carefully studied this subject with a sincere desire to find out if I could, why it was that this difficulty to which my hon. friend refers between the generals who come here, imperial officers, and Ministers of Militia and Defence in this country should recur over and over again in this country. I have come to the conclusion that the reason of it is that the imperial officers who come here have no experience which would fit them to deal with the government of the day. They come here as imperial officers, having lived for a long time in a very narrow sphere where they have learned nothing but to command, being also under the command of a superior officer-not even having had the opportunity of having served in permanent positions in the war office where they would be brought in contact with the executive government, with the War Minister. They come to this country therefore without the experience which would fit them for a position directly under a minister who is responsible to the parliament and the people of Canada. They have not even had the advantage of occupying a position near the executive of the mother country. How much less, then, can we expect them to immediately accommodate themselves to occupying a subordinate position in a colonial administration. Now, Mr. Speaker, this, I believe, is the cause of the serious difficulties we have had; and I am afraid that, until the time comes when a different class of officers, men who have had experience in the war office and in touch with the executive of England, are sent to this country, these difficulties will recur over and over again. The general 76}
officer commanding the militia of this country is an imperial officer, it is true and must have rank not below that of colonel in the British army. Why is that made, a provision of the Canadian Militia Law ? Simply and solely because it is thought that it may be presumed to secure the necessary qualification to enable him to command an army in this country, and for no other reason. When he leaves the British army for the time being and comes to this country, he comes here as the official of the Dominion government, he comes under Order in Council appointing him by the Governor General of Canada, and is the officer and official of the Canadian government and responsible to the Canadian government and the Canadian people alone. Do not let us misunderstand this point-that although he is an imperial officer, that fact does not give him any additional power or authority in this country. Now, I do not know that it is necessary for me to enlarge. I will simply conclude what I have to say by reading again what was said in this House by the Prime Minister in 1900, on the occasion of the difficulty that occurred with Major General Hutton :
The government desire to state that while they will, at all times, be prepared to give the most careful consideration to any representations which may be made by the officer commanding the militia, it must be distinctly understood that any such officer, on accepting the position in question becomes from that time an officer in the employment of and subject in all respects to the government of Canada, and that he is to be regarded as an adviser but not as entitled to control the Department of Militia. The government are responsible to the parliament and people of Canada for the due administration of each and every branch of the public service, and they would be derelict in their duty if they were to permit any subordinate official, under any circumstances, to take upon himself to disregard the instructions he may receive from the constitutional head of his department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden).

speechtext:
I am delighted to hear the Minister of Militia reiterate the words prepared, I believe by the hon. and gallant gentleman who fills the position of Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) and voiced by the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier). It took the ministry a long time to learn their duty in the premises. A struggle went on with that offic'er -I refer to General Hutton. He tyrannized over the Minister of Militia, he tyrannized over the Prime Minister, he even undertook to manage those higher in authority. But I claim the credit of having taught the country what the duty of a general officer commanding in Canada ought to be. But I was not supported. I regret to say that I was deserted by my own friends, and I was not reinforced by the present government. I fought the fight single-handed on that occasion. The voice of my good friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) was unheard.

He was silent. To-day, when we have a general officer commanding who is a gentleman, when we have a general officer commanding who has won his laurels on the fields of fame, when we have a general officer commanding who lives within the constitution, we find that lion, gentleman rising in his seat and slinging mud at him.
Now, Sir, the hon. gentleman has complained of the language made use of hy Lord Duudonald in the city of Hamilton. Lord Duudonald gave utterance to no language that was confidential; he expressed no opinion there which had not been officially reported to his minister, and that had not been endorsed by his minister; and I believe, and am credibly informed by gentlemen who were there, that when the Postmaster General got through reading his carefully prepared essay on militarism at the banquet in Hamilton, he found his utterances received so coldly that even he swung round and endorsed the remarks made by the general officer commanding. At all events, I find by the newspapers published in the city of Hamilton, Liberals and Conservatives alike, that the Hon. Col. Gibson rose in his place and endorsed most cordially the remarks of the general officer commanding. Lord Dundonald did not seek to override the minister in the slightest degree. But we found the ministers, and we find the followers of the government, sitting dumb in their seats when a former general officer commanding did seek to override the Minister of Militia, and in fact did override the whole ministry. Lord Dundonald did not treat the Minister of Militia as an inferior and refuse to obey his orders. Lord Dundonald has never undertaken to place a curb on any member of the House of Commons; he has never undertaken to control the action or the language of any military member of this House of Commons on military questions; yet this was done, to the knowledge of the ministry, by the former general officer commanding, and not one word was uttered on the floor of this House or elsewhere in this country, so far as known in condemnation of that policy. Lord Dundonald lias never had the audacity to approach His Excellency over the head of his minister, and! to receive and transmit commands from His Excellency to officers of the militia of this country. Were he to do that, I am satisfied he would be dismissed. But a former general officer commanding did do it, and did it with the knowledge of the government, and he was not checked for it by the government. Lord Dundonald has never attempted either to communicate officially with the war office in the old country. I fail to see why this officer should be brought up before the country to-day and be treated in the manner in which the hon. member for Labelle has undertaken to treat him here to-day. I must congratulate the minister though in this regard, that he has treated Lord Dundonald very fairly, and

although there may be a little hidden menace in the note of warning he read at the conclusion of his address, I must congratulate the minister on his treatment of the general officer commanding.
Now X noticed in the essay read by the Postmaster General at Hamilton, a very beautiful essay, that he discussed most eloquently the curse of militarism. Let me point out to that hon. gentleman that when he speaks of the ' northern hemisphere '-I presume he meant the western hemisphere, but the newspapers credited him with saying the northern hemisphere-when he refers to the United States of America ns a nation indulging in the arts of peace and whose footsteps we should follow, let me tell him that, starting from the year 1783 when the United States first gained its independence down to a time subsequent to the Boer war, the United States has spent millions of dollars more on war than have Great Britain and all her colonies combined. I have the figures, and shall be pleased to submit them to the House if required, or to the minister on any occasion. More than that. I; want to point out to him that Britain's prestige to-day, Britain's civilization to-day, Britain's Christianity to-day, are due to her power in war; and I have yet to see the nation that has earned greatness in commerce, greatness in art, greatness in anything that goes to make a nation illustrious, that has not owed it primarily to her military prowess. I am prepared to discuss that question whenever it is necessary so to do. It is only in recent years that Great Britain has given way to the spirit of militarism.
Take the speech of Lord Dundonald at Hamilton, and compare it with the essay of the Postmaster General. Sir, I maintain that, on the one hand, the remarks of Lord Dundonald breathed the true spirit for a democratic country to adopt. Train up the militia of the country, make its organization as perfect as possible, and you will prevent the spirit of militarism from becoming dominant in that country. You will find that the rank and file of the people, the boys on the farm, the young men in the workshops of the cities and towns, will be a military people, they will be military men in their capacity as citizens. But the policy propounded by the Postmaster General has bred in all countries a spirit of militarism and exclusiveness, that has built up tyrannies the world over; for we find that in these countries where a citizen soldiery has been neglected, tyrannies rise much more easily than they do in those countries where the rank and file of the people are trained in their duties as citizen soldiers.
In the remarks made by Lord Dundonald at the meeting of the Dominion Rifle Association, the Minister of Militia was present, and I am satisfied he will bear me out in saying that the remarks of the general officer commanding did not at all permit the

construction placed upon them by my hon. friend from Labelle. He referred jocularly to the expenditure of $13,000,000 in the development of militia. Supposing we armed the, people of Canada, I would like to see 150,000 rifles, I would like to see 500,000 rifles placed in the hands of the farmer's sons of Canada by the government. Let them be placed with the boys on the farms and with the people generally, under any proper system of control. What would these rifles cost ? Multiply each one by $25, and you will have the figures, nearly the full amount of that $13,000,000. Then supposing you were to have a few more batteries of artillery, a few more regiments of cavalry, and you will reach beyond the $13,000,000 at once. But once these expenditures are incurred, they need not be repeated for a great many years.
It has been made public in some unofficial way that Lord Dundonald has recommended an expenditure of $13,000,000, and I have demanded that his report shall be made public officially so that the public may have an opportunity of knowing what his recommendations are. I can readily figure out that for placing this country in a better state of preparedness and for providing the necessary armament for the defence of a young nation such as this an expenditure, extending over a number of years, of course, involving a number of millions of dollars could very properly and very usefully be indulged in. However, it is not my intention at this period of the session to discuss this question any further.
I must congratulate the lion. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden) on his endorsement of the course of Lord Dundonald. Mark you, if I found Lord Dundonald, or any imperial or Canadian officer, encroaching upon the rights of citizenship, encroaching upon the rights of the people's representatives in this House, I would be one of the first to bring him to time, but I have watched Lord Duudonald's course very carefully, and I have seen nothing to find fault with in it. In South Africa he was a gentleman ; he treated the officers and men under him as gentlemen and soldiers, and they followed him as a leader. In this country Lord Dundonald has not once encroached upon the domain of the minister. He has been in every respect, so far as I can judge, a model general officer commanding, recognizing that he is the servant of a responsible government and that the minister is responsible to the people of the country. On another occasion, when the Bill of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence comes down, we will have an opportunity of discussing these matters at greater length, but in the meantime, I wish to express my disapprobation of the line of action pursued by the hon. member for Labelle in bringing this matter up and seeking to cast a reflection upon the general officer commanding. When I heard of the
matter first I did not know what Lord Dundonald had said in Hamilton, but I got the papers and read them over very carefully, and I was more than surprised to find that he had kept himself so well under control, and that he had not referred to one solitary matter that the minister had not cordially endorsed his position upon.

I do not rise, Mr. Speaker, to attempt any defence of Lord Dundonald. It seems to me that is quite unnecessary, especially after what I think are the very proper remarks of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Hon. Sir Frederick Borden). I happened to be chairman of the banquet in Hamilton, and as I paid very particular attention to the language of Lord Dundonald on that Occasion, I confess that it was with the utmost surprise that I heard that the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) thought of bringing forward this question in the House. If that hon. gentleman had been present, I think he would have admitted that there was not a syllable uttered at that banquet by Lord Dundonald which might not have been uttered had the hon. minister been at his side. Lord Dundonald, I may say, was there as one of three guests who were invited from a distance by the St. George's Society. Lord Dundonald was one, the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mtilock) was another, and my hon. friend the member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) was another. On that occasion Lord Dundonald was called upon to respond to the toast of 'Our Defenders.' In the course of his response he referred to his service in South Africa, and particularly, when alluding in the usual terms to the regular forces, the army and navy, he dwelt upon the colonial volunteers, and he especially mentioned in the warmest terms that gallant regiment the Strathcona Horse. He said that it had been an honour for him to have included in his brigade in South Africa the Canadian regiment called the Strathconas ; and I mention that particularly in consequence of a few words that fell from the hon. minister, and because Lord Dundonald appears in South Africa to have had under his command a large force of colonial troops, which experience, I should think, makes him most fittingly the right man in the right place in Canada. Lord Dundonald, when alluding in the usual terms to the troops, added some words upon the experiences he had had in Natal, and in referring to the miseries of the people there, he said that the lesson they had learned in that province was to organize in good time and not wait for the bursting of the storm. He at the same time said he thought it would be well if the people of Canada and if the militia of Canada, a large number of officers being present and listening to him, would take the lesson to heart and see that the militia force was made effective. Lord

Dundonald, from first to last, never used one word upon the policy of this country as to the militia. He never departed from mere questions of detail. There was not a word uttered from first to last as to the numbers of the militia, as to whether the force should be increased, or as to any such question of policy. But he did say that what he desired to see was that the militia of Canada should be effective, that if, under any unfortunate circumstances, the militia were called out and regiments brigaded, it was his desire that they could be turned out ready in every particular to do their duty. In this connection he mentioned two or three matters of detail, and these were the particular matters upon which his speech chiefly ran. He said, first of all, there was the question of transport, and he thought it was of the utmost importance that this question of transport should be considered and that the force should be fully equipped for service in that respect. Judging by the response which the officers present gave to that remark, I think they all agreed with him. He further said it was of importance that the force should be educated in signalling, that the officers should be so taught that a general in command of a brigade, or of any body of troops, could flash his orders to the heads of the component parts of the brigade. The appliances for that purpose should be provided and officers commanding should be so instructed that they would understand the signals when they got them. I think that also received the approbation of all who heard it. He referred to the field telegraph, the heliograph and other matters of that kind, and his speech was confined soley to such matters. Judging by the demonstrations and comments of those who were listening, and they were prominent people belonging to the city of Hamilton and officers of the local force'and from the neighbouring towns, I think his remarks were received with unanimous approval. He deprecated anything like militarism ; he did this more than once ; but he said, as has been quoted here to-day : That he thought the matters he was trying to impress upon his audience were matters of common sense, and he urged them merely as matters of detail regarding the force as it exists, and not at all as undertaking to urge that any other or larger force should be created. The Postmaster General (Hon. Sir Wm. Mulock) followed in response to another toast, and he also deprecated militarism, but I did not understand the Postmaster General to take exception to any remark made by the Major General Commanding. I quote from a newspaper one remark made by the Postmaster General, and apparently uttered by him to show that he was not taking exception to what Lord Dundonald said. He said :
I refer not to measures of defence, but to that aggressive warlike spirit known as militarism.

The Postmaster General was condemning the aggressive, warlike spirit known as militarism, but he was not condemning defence, and the Major General was commenting upon the organization of our troops as a defensive body and urging that they should be equipped most thoroughly for that purpose. The Attorney General for Ontario was present, and I think he is as good a Liberal as the member for Labelle or any member of this House. Speaking after the Postmaster General and the Major General, the Hon. Mr. Gibson said :
The gist of Lord Dundonald's argument was well expressed when His Lordship said : ' As citizen soldiers what was wanted was organization.'
There is the language of the Attorney General for Ontario, who understood perfectly what the Major General was referring to under the term ' organization.' Lord Dundonald was not speaking of organizing the people of Canada into a military force, but of organizing the force that exists ; a force which this government and all preceding governments have conceded is a necessity for this country. Lord Dundonald argued, that that force, proud as we are of it, is lacking in some respects, and he wanted to see it up to date in every respect, so that if called upon it would, as he said, spring out ready equipped for duty on the bell being pushed. The Attorney General of Ontario is an old parliamentarian and he used this language further :
As commander of the militia Lord Dundonald was the right man in the right place. While the General Commanding and the Postmaster General had reached the same conclusion he had to admit that they argued along different lines.
The only difference between them was that the Postmaster General was speaking of the blessings of peace, and he did so most eloquently, but he carefully guarded himself , from saying one word against the argument that had been used with regard to defence.
I do not know that I need say any more.
It is a painful thing that any gentleman who was a guest on that occasion and who used language that no person could take exception to, should have his name brought up in this House as if he were guilty of some indiscretion.
Hear, hear.

As one who was present and knowing how utterly undeserved is the language used in regard to that gallant soldier, I say it is a painful thing that this matter should be brought before the House in this way. Lord Dundonald was kind enough to come all the way to Hamilton as a guest of St. George's Society. He did so at a great deal of inconvenience to himself and he was most guarded in the language he used. It is unfortunate that his name should be mentioned in this House in connection with a supposed impropriety such

as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou-rassa) imagines. Now, Sir, I may say with regard to the general subject of the right of a commanding officer to speak on such an occasion, it does seem to me most extraordinary that a member of this House should think that the Major General should have his tongue tied, and should not be allowed to express an opinion, even on matters of detail with regard to our militia force. Surely, the superintendent of our farms, in making a speech at some banquet, would not be condemned because he would advocate farming up to date, or, if he said jocularly that he hoped the government farm would get a little of that $13,000,000. Suppose the manager of our railways was making a speech at a banquet and he advocated railway appliances up to date, would it be expected that the Minister of Railways should turn upon him and say : You had no right to speak, sir ; you must not utter a word in public ; you must let me speak for you. Surely gentlemen who are charged with most important public interests, whether as commanding our militia force, or as controlling departments under ministers, have some right to express their opinions. What is the good of them if they do not form opinions, and if they do form them, why not tell us what they are ? We are expending something like $2,000,000 a year on our military force, and is the man who tells us that we should have that force, which costs us so much, properly equipped and efficient, but that it is not so ; is he to be condemned if he expresses that opinion ? I hope not, Sir.
Hear, hear.
Mr. Speaker. I am essentially a man of peace.
Hear, hear.

And although I believe that under the terms of the statute, I belong to the militia of Canada, I do not rise with any idea of criticising our military organization. But, as having been one of the guests at the banquet at Hamilton, I feel it almost a duty to confirm what has just been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Barker), the member for that city. I may say, Sir, that sitting alongside of the general officer commanding, I lent particular attention to every word that fell from his lips, and in anything which he said I did not notice a word that would lead one to believe that it was his desire to innovate in any way and still less to dictate to the administration the line of conduct it ought to pursue in respect to military organization. The general officer commanding began by stating that what few remarks he had to offer he wished to confine them exclusively to the efficiency of the militia force as it exists. He spoke of the importance, in a large country like ours, of having our militia men conversant with the signalling system; he spoke
of the necessity of proper accommodation for the militia; he spoke of the necessity, demonstrated during the late war in South Africa, of practice in rifle shooting ; and he did say-and it seemed to me he advisedly said-that we should have such a militia organization that would admit of it being placed at a moment's notice upon a proper footing of defence. Beyond that, he mentioned the conduct of our own troops in South Africa and gave us some very interesting reminiscences of his own experiences during the war; and I feel bound to render him the tribute of justice which I am doing in confirmation of what has been said by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). I am happy, in the absence of the general officer commanding, who is not able to defend himself in this House, to render him this tribute, that he impressed me as being not only a very brave man, but a man of very modest and unassuming demeanour.
I do not think any person in this House will call in question what was laid down by the hon. Minister of Militia, and what was insisted on at perhaps unnecessary length by my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bour-assa), that we have absolute control of our own militia organization. There is no doubt on that point; and, for my own part, referring more particularly to the explanatory remarks made to-day by the hon. Minister of Militia, and in spite of what has been said here on more than one occasion by my hon. friend from Gasp6 (Mr. Le-mieux), I have always adhered to the hope that at some date not too distant-and I have expressed this hope at different places in my own province and elsewhere-it will be possible for us to have at the head of our military organization some man of Canadian birth and origin. In the meantime, however, I think it is only justice that we should not rashly attack in this House statements made at public meetings by men of the high standing and reputation of the general officer commanding, whom I had the honour of meeting in the city of Hamilton.
I do not concur in the opinion expressed here by my hon. friend from Labelle, that a general officer commanding, coming to this country under the circumstances which we know, occupies absolutely the same position as a deputy minister of militia or some ordinary head of a department. I do not think the government would subscribe to the proposition. My hon. friend from Labelle must not forget that statements made at the colonial conference by the members of the administration, who represented us on that occasion, as contained in the blue-book published by the British government, and which I regret very much to say, our own government have not seen fit to give us communication of. In the blue-book we find it stated that the Prime Minister at the colonial conference declared that it was the intention of our own government to organize a naval force here. I find in the

memorandum submitted by our own ministers, at page 74, the following statement:
In conclusion the ministers represent that while the Canadian government are obliged to dissent from the measures proposed

These were measures of regular organization for defence.
-they fully Erppreciate the obligation of the Dominion to make expenditures for the purposes of defence in proportion to the increasing population and wealth of the country. They are willing that these expenditures shall be so directed as to relieve the taxpayer in the mother country from some of the burdens which he now bears, and they have the strongest desire to carry out their defence schemes in cooperation with the imperial authorities and under the advice of experienced imperial officers, so far as this is consistent with the principle of local self-government, which has proved so great a factor in the promotion of imperial unity.
Now, Sir, after that statement by our ministers at the colonial conference, and submitted in writing, I do not think we should be easily disposed to find fault with an experienced imperial officer coming out here, who is invited to a banquet, and who suggests such improvements and reforms in the militia as were suggested at the banquet in Hamilton by the general officer commanding. I should add, before taking my seat, that after the hon. Postmaster General had expressed his own views to that important gathering, he turned to the general officer commanding and stated that none of the remarks which he himself had just made should be construed in any sense as being a contradiction of what had been said by the general officer commanding, with whose views he was in perfect accord. Under these circumstances. I felt that it was my duty to render to a man whom I was proud to meet, that tribute of justification which I have taken the liberty to render to-day.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. T. THOMPSON (Haldimand and Monck).
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I feel that the subject before the House has been pretty thoroughly exhausted, and I would take no part in the debate but for the feeling of deep respect which I entertain towards the general officer commanding, Lord Dundonald. I was sorry indeed that the hon. member for Labelle saw fit to bring this matter before the House, and in a manner which I think made it little less than an attack on the general officer commanding. As usual, I think that hon. member was constitutionally right and otherwise wrong. I do not think anybody will be found in this House or out of it, to challenge the position he takes, that the militia policy of this country must be dictated by the government of the country. But who was attacking that principle ? Did Lord Dundonald attack it in one single utterance of those which the hon. gentleman quoted ? I happened myself to be present at the meeting of the Dominion Rifle Association at which Lord Dundonald delivered

a speech from which the hon. member for Labelle quoted. Lord Dundonald was merely meeting and repelling an attack which had been made upon him by some of the newspapers of Canada. One of them had said that he was recommending an expenditure of $12,000,000 in one year on the Canadian militia. This was doing nothing more nor less than holding him up to ridicule in Canada. All of us know that an expenditure of that kind would be impossible in this country, and to suggest it would stamp a man as completely out of touch with the public sentiment of this country and ignorant of the resources of the country. Lord Dundonald merely said that he had made no such suggestion, but that the money might be spent in three or four years to advantage, and so it might. The hon. member for Labelle professed to be only discussing the constitutional question ; but he did not confine himself to that, but undertook to criticise the statements of Lord Dundonald, and went on to say, with a great deal of glee and merriment, that Lord Dundonald admitted that he was willing to spend that sum in three or four years. And yet the hon. member for Labelle himself- and I always listen to him with attention-said on this very floor that he would recommend the government of Canada to take over the defences of Halifax and Esquimalt. Does he know what that means ? Does he know that 1,600 British troops are at Halifax now, and that a fortification, for its size one of the strongest in the world, christened Spion Kopje, has lately been built there by the British government at a very large cost ? Does he know that the defences of Esquimalt involve a further cost of hundreds and thousands of dollars, and that the expendiutre involved in taking over these two defences, which he advocates, would probably be as much as he criticised Lord Dundonald for having hinted at.
Still the hon. member for Labelle went further and said that he was in accord with the feeling in this country that the militia of Canada should be put on a suitable basis. Does the hon. gentleman know what that means ? Those of us who have studied the subject realize that we require a very great deal in Canada to put the militia on a proper basis. I do not know that we really need 500,000 rifles in Canada as suggested by the hon. member for Victoria. X think that we could get along with a few less, although as rifles are liable to get out of order, it might be as well to have considerably more than the 40.000 now in our armouries ? Of what use to have 100,000 trained men and not enough rifles to go around ? We cannot fight with pitch forks at two thousand yards. I think that we might also spend a little more money in increasing the armaments of this country. X do not think that there is anything very ridiculous in that proposition, and I believe that the hon. member for Labelle, in advo-

As extracts from the report which appeared in the Hamilton ' Times ' of the speech delivered by Lord Dundonald on the 23rd of April have been read to the House and comments made on them, it is only due to that gallant officer that I should quote the full report of the speech he made, and with your permission, Sir, 1 would like to do so. Lord Dundonald said :
His Lordship said that he would not be able to reply to the toast in the eloquent words in which it had been proposed. It was a big subject and it included the soldiers of the empire, whose drum beat was heard around the globe. His Lordship referred to the assistance Canada had given to the mother country in the South African war. He had in his command Lord Strathcona's Horse. He never had such eager men in his command. His chief trouble was to hold them back. He spoke feelingly of the Canadians who had given their lives for the empire, and he made reference to the bad news of yesterday from Somaliland. He had confidence the memory of the disaster would be wiped out by British troops.
Lord Dundonald spoke of the campaign in Natal during the recent Boer war, and he referred to some of the scenes through which his troops passed. He believed the lessons of the war were being considered, and ihe people of South Africa were putting their house in order. He thought the people of Canada also were considering the lessons of the war, and they had learned that the time to organize was before the storm broke-not afterwards. What he would like to see in the country was a condition in which when he pressed the button the regiments throughout Canada would turn out at once.
Was this the case now ? Lord Dundonald said that it was necessary to have a better system of transport. How was Canada equipped in this respect ? Would any hon. member say that in drawing attention to these matters, the general officer commanding our forces was not acting within his duty ? Would any hon. member be disposed to censure him for drawing attention to what he considered a matter of urgency ? Then, after pointing out the various ways in which improvements could be made, he proceeded to say, according to this report :
The Canadian militia had had as their diet promises instead of food ; praise instead of wine. What was wanted was a little of thai $13,000,000 surplus. A bugbear of militarism was not wanted, but an efficient force-efficient in organization, in its departments, and efficient in its system of leaders. The modern rifle had given to small nations a power they never had before, but it also gave an aggressor power to hold what he seized. It was the duty of all men in the nation to study military matters, so they would know what was needed for the good of the country.
In his opinion the northern nations of the earth must be the dominant nations. The men of the north, who were brought up amid the hardening conditions of ice and snow must be superior to those raised in the balmier climate of the south.
His Lordship said it was a great pleasure to him to he present at a St. George's dinner. It was the first time for him to dine at a St. George's banquet, but he had been at a St. Andrew's festival gathering. He thanked the St. George's Society for having invited him to the city.
After listening to the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle, I could not help asking myself whether we were really In one of the free parliaments of the British empire this afternoon. How any Canadian subject, who desires to see the militia of this country made as efficient as possible, could take the slightest exception to the remarks of Lord Dundonald I fail to understand. I thought that the remarks of the hon. member for Labelle were very farfetched. At that banquet were present my hon. friend the Postmaster General (Hon. Sir William Mulock), my hon. friend for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), my hon. friend the Attorney General of Ontario, Mr. Gibson, and the hon. members who represent the city of Hamilton in this House, every one of whom is just as jealous of the honour and prero-

gatives of the parliament of Canada as the hon. member for Labelle can possibly be. Had the general officer commanding given expression to opinions or sentiments "that he should not, every one of these hon. gentlemen would have been willing and anxious to set him right, if not to take him to task. What did the hon. Attorney General of Ontario say ? He said :
While the general officer commanding and the Postmaster General had reached the same natural conclusion, he had to admit that they had argued along different lines.
If an officer who occupies the position of the general officer commanding the militia forces of Canada, and who is an
imperial officer, is not permitted to express his opinions regarding the position in which he finds our militia, and to make suggestions among a company of Canadian gentlemen gathered together at a St. George's banquet, I am at a loss to know what freedom of action his duty to this country will allow him. Surely the remarks he made were merely personal expressions of opinion, in no way reflecting on the policy of the Militia Department; and it seems to me that it was clearly out of place for the hon. member for Labelle to challenge these remarks, because, as the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat has said, they are endorsed by all the members with the single exception of the hon. gentleman who takes exception to them. I think that the record of Lord Dondonald, the record of the services he has performed, the fact that he is the worthy head of a great clan, and the worthy representative of a great nation which has given so many soldiers and sailors to the empire, the fact that he has stated nothing contrary to the interests of the Canadian militia, the fact that he has in no way interfered with the prerogative of the Minister of Militia and Defence or of this parliament, should have protected him from the assault which has been made upon him this afternoon And I. for one, hope, Mr. Speaker, that this is the last occasion when, on such a flimsy pretext, such a discussion as the present will be raised in this House. I desire to congratulate, and congratulate most heartily, the Minister of Militia and Defence on the stand he took in this case. It is high time that officers who come from the old land, who are British subjects like ourselves, should be protected in giving expression to their opinions on matters on which they are competent to form an opinion, and "they should not be attacked for giving to the Canadian people advice which will enable them to make the militia force of Canada a force efficient in every respect. The Minister of Militia and Defence will admit, and every military gentleman in this House will admit, that every word stated by the officer commanding respecting our miiitia force is true. Will any hon. gentleman who has had experience in militia matters contra-, Mr. CLARKE.
diet one single statement to which the general officer commanding gave utterance ? If not, the time of this House should not be wasted ; and the character and reputation and rights of honourable gentlemen and gallant soldiers who cannot come here to defend themselves should be protected. The House should frown down these exhibitions which are calculated to do harm and which certainly cannot do good.

I rise with some diffidence to speak in this debate; for my military days are over. There was a time when I was more warlike and would not have hesitated to shoulder the musket, but I have now reached an age when I have been placed upon the ' reserve.' I would not take part in the debate except for the warm manner in which my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has addressed the House. I must say that I do not think the strictures which he passed upon my hon. friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) were at all called for. I do not take it that my hon. friend from Labelle took exception to the sentiments uttered by Lord Dun-donald, but I understood him to say that he thought that Lord Dundonald was trying to dictate to the policy of the government.
I do not think his criticism went further. Whether the conclusion reached by my hon. friend (Mr. Bourassa) was warranted or not,
I do not know, because, I must confess, I did not read at the time the words of Lord Dundonald. Of course, Lord Dundonald is a brave officer ; he has made liis career and proved his courage, and I believe that he is able and painstaking. So far, I agree with my hon. friend from West Toronto. But, I must say that the gentleman who commands the militia of Canada whatever may have been his services elsewhere, is always amenable to public opinion as expressed in parliament. Whether his services are meritorious or otherwise, whether he is right or wrong, it is the privilege of any member of this House to call his actions in question. And I must say to my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) that if we are to doubt to-day whether we are in a British parliament or not, the doubt does not arise from anything spoken by my hon. friend from Labelle, but from what has been spoken by my hon. friend from West Toronto. I have the greatest respect for the gentleman commanding the militia, as much as my hon. friend (Mr. Clarke) has. I think he is one of the ablest men we have ever had to perform this important duty.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: And he is a gentleman.

He is a gentleman in every sense of the word. Whether we should have a Canadian or imperial officer as our commander of militia. I will not discuss now. But, whatever may be the merits of the officer commanding the mill-

tia, lie is a subordinate of the Canadian government, and, if be has any policy to propound, it should be propounded to the minister, and the minister is responsible.
He did not propound any policy.

If there were any doubt, I have only to say that we have the same privilege in this House that they have in the British parliament, and there is no doubt whatever that a general commanding the forces has no right to give advice to the people. If he has advice to give, he must give it, not to the people but to the minister whose officer he is. If the General Commanding the Militia has advice to tender, it is not his right-I say it deliberately-to offer advice to the public, but it is his duty to offer it to the minister, and for that policy the minister shall be responsible. The principles are too elementary to be contradicted, but I thought, after the expressions of my hon. friend from West Toronto, it was not inadvisable to repeat them to the House, and even to himself.

If this war like episode is over, perhaps I may be permitted to refer to the matter that I attempted to bring up when the Orders of the Day were called, the mutilation of the beautiful lawn on the parliament grounds. I noticed yesterday some nine or ten men working on it cutting off the sod, and to-day they have horses and carts drawing the sods away. My first impression was that they intended to attempt some ornamentation with flower beds. But, on making inquiries, I was surprised to find that the object was to make cricket ground for the benefit of the youthful members of the Senate and the House of Commons. I have known for some time that it was the desire of the present government to reform the Senate, but I did not think that that reform would take this direction. They have put in the Senate so many youthful gentlemen between the ages of sixty-five and eighty-five that now they seem to think it necessary to spend public money to make a recreation ground to keep them in good condition mentally and physically. I regret this very much, because it seems to me this mutilation is more like vandalism than anything else. A few years ago, we had the diagonal paths across the grounds, and I do not think they were an element of besyity by any means. It was decided, in the wisdom of those who control these matters, to fill up these paths, and that was done at considerable expense, I thought the result was a very beautiful landscape. When I see the sod cut off to make a cricket ground at an expense to the country of $150 to $200, I confess the wisdom of such a step
is beyond my comprehension. If it is absolutely necessary that we should have cricket why should not the members of parliament, and senators go to Cartier Square and amuse themselves there ? I wonder how far we are to go in these matters. We cannot stop at making grounds. After they are made, we must have an item in the estimates to buy leggings, balls, bats and all the necessary equipment, including clothing, for a proper and respectable parliamentary team, that, I suppose, may travel over the country. I object to this kind of thing all the more because of the parsimony of the government has led them to refuse us anything except an ordinary table in a room. We have been refused a desk, a cupboard or anything where one could store one's letters and lock them up, because you, Mr. Speaker, tell us that the government's desire is to exercise the most stringent economy in connection with the affairs of this House. If a little were saved out of the expense of making a parliamentary cricket grounds and we were given ordinary conveniences to carry on our parliamentry work, it would be better. I think that the government, having their attention directed to this matter, ought to put a stop to this work. I don't think that is right, I don't think the country should endorse it. I do not think that it is right that the beautiful landscape we have had heretofore should be destroyed for the purpose of giving a few youthful members of parliament and senators physical exercise.

Although I have already spoken, I may be pardoned for speaking again on this subject. It so seldom happens that I can agree with my hon. friend from Grey (Sir. Sproule) that I desire to say that on this occasion I agree with everything that he has said. I do not know that his remarks will be approved by the Minister of Public Works, but I shall convey to him the remarks of my hon. friend, along with my own strong endorsation of his view in favour of keeping the lawn.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext:
McCarthy (North Simcoe). It seems to me that the parsimony of which the hon. member for East Grey complains as existing in the government, exists rather in the heart of the hon. member himself. It is true, I believe, that some members representing both sides of the House spoke to the Minister of Public Works, and pointed out that the grass on the spot where improvements are now going on was not in very good condition. He and his officers looked at it and came to the same conclusion. A small sum of money, not so large as the hon. member has stated, is being spent there for the purpose of improving the ground. But it will not be left in the condition in which it is now, it is going to ba sodded so that a game of cricket can be

played upon It. To suggest that playing cricket upon the grass in front of this House is a work of vandalism, is more I think than the free British people in this Canada of ours will uphold. Now, it is just as easy for us to improve our bodies by playing cricket as it is to improve our minds by sitting in the House of Commons and listening to the hon. gentleman's speeches. It is sometimes necessary to seek recreation for the purpose of bracing one's self up after listening to the speeches of the hon. member for East Grey. As to his complaint about parsimony, I presume that if something was done to some room or other in the Commons, if the desk which he says he cannot get were supplied, possibly he would shut his eyes and wink at the expenditure which has been made for the benefit of the whole parliament. I do not wonder that the hon. gentleman is somewhat jealous, because he would have you understand that a room which he himself occupies is not furnished as he would desire. I have been in the rooms of some of the hon. members on that side of the House, and I have seen them very well furnished, a great deal better furnished than some of the rooms of hon. members on the government side. So possibly it is jealousy which exists in the mind of the hon. member whom the Minister of Customs referred to the other night as the opposition leader from Ontario. Now I believe this is the extent of his complaint, that if we went to the Minister of Public Works and asked him to give the hon. gentleman a desk, or a chair, or a sofa, which would probably cost $100 or $150, he would probably wink at it, and would not mind the expense of the improvements on the lawn in frout of the House. Now cricket is known to be a game in which the Britisher delights, and I should think that improving ourselves in that way would meet the approval of the hon. gentleman. I would ask him if he does not approve of a game which improves the strength of a senator who may bo between the years of sixty-five and eighty-five, as well as the strength of those representing a younger branch of the legislature. I think that we may all be permitted to enjoy a game of cricket, without in any way damaging the beauty of the lawn in front of the House.

As one of the cricketers, I would like to say a word as to the improvement that is in progress on the lawn. I should like also to allay the anxiety of the hon. member for East Grey in regard to the desecration. I think when the hon. member sees a game going on there, he will be inclined to come and join us himself. I approve of this small expenditure which is entailed by the new sodding, because I believe that cricket is a good thing for us young members, at any rate, and perhaps for some of the older members of the House, if they would join with us. It Mr. McCarthy.
would be very advantageous to our health, if we are going to be kept here during the summer, that we should be provided with some recreation of that kind. I am sure that the small expenditure that is being made by the Minister of Public Works will not be found fault with by our constituents in the country.

Yesterday I gave notice to the government that when the House was next moved into Committee of Supply I would bring up the matter of the Treadgold concessions. But at the request of certain hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who wish to speak on this question, and as the Minister of the Interior is not here, I readily acquiesced in the request for delay that has been made, with the understanding that the question will be taken up to-morrow.

I am sorry to say that I do not think it will be possible for it to come up to-morrow. We have some important Bills which will take up the time to-morrow. But if they are disposed of, we will be only too glad to give an opportunity to my hon. friend.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Now that the very important question of military propriety raised by my hon. friend for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), and I suppose the equally important question raised by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) have been settled to the satisfaction of the House, I desire to draw your attention for a few minutes to another important matter, that is the congestion of the railway traffic which prevails in this country. That congestion now prevails to a serious extent in the western part of Canada, and has prevailed for the past twenty months. In place of the situation improving as the months go by, the people in western Canada find that the traffic congestion is becoming still more serious, and it has reached a state now when I am warranted in bringing it to the attention of the House and of the government. I ask the pardon of the House for reading at some length newspaper statements, and some documents bearing upon the question, which are calculated to lead the House to realize the gravity of the question. In the issue of a Regina newspaper dated the 30th of April, I find an article headed

Yards Choked with Traffic-Merchants Suffering from Ruinous Delays.
For many weeks past first one merchant and then another has in vigorous language drawn the attention of ' The Leader ' to "lie tact that

the condition of railway traffic in the west is continually getting worse. The situation last year was bad enough when for days and sometimes weeks merchants would be completely out of certain lines of goods because the railway could not get them in, but this year it is infinitely worse for many business houses have been completely sold out of certain lines for weeks and months, notwithstanding that their orders had been placed in plenty of time and the goods promptly shipped by the wholesalers in the east. There is to-day hardly a merchant in Regina-and our exchanges tell the same story of all parts of the territories-who has not orders for goods which were promptly shipped now long overdue. Merchants who ordered goods for the Christmas trade received them after that festive season was over and had to dispose of them at a sacrifice. Others who had supplies ordered and shipped for the early spring trade will have to carry them over for a whole year. The situation at present is that so unreliable has the freight service become that merchants are afraid to place large orders for certain seasonable goods not knowing but they will arrive after the opportune season is past. Any supplies which must be secured without a delay of a month or more are ordered to be shipped by express. This of necessity makes a ruinous inroad into the profits.
A representative spent a short time on Tuesday in going over the Canadian Pacific Railway yard here. By actual count there were over 200 freight cars on the sidings, not taking into account engines, tenders, water tank cars, cabooses and passenger coaches. Cattle cars were to be seen loaded with coal, some of which had not been cleaned before loading, while Lemp's brewery car was labelled as being loaded with lumber from British Columbia. Some of these cars have been in the yard for weeks and were as yet unloaded because they had not been placed where teams could get at them. The yard wa,s so badly congested, almost every foot of track on the sidings being taken up with cars, that it was practically impossible to place cars and in one part of the yard a gang of men were unloading goods on to the prairie. Here was a miscellaneous collection of stoves and other hardware, dry goods, drugs, books and stationery, confectionery and candies, &c., some of which had been on the way to Regina for a couple of months past. In another part of the yard a gang of men were at work laying more track.
On Sunday, the 19th inst., a gentleman counted 123 cars in the gravel pit at Pilot Butte, eight miles east of here

I may say that Pilot Butte is simply a flag station.
-and many of these were consigned to Regina and had been in the pit for weeks. One of the Regina carters has made numerous trips to Pilot Butte in order to dray goods into town. One case may be cited of goods ordered of a Toronto firm by telegraph from Regina on February 21st for immediate shipment, a portion of which was delivered here on April 25th ; the balance Is yet to come. These goods were in the Pilot Butte gravel pit for some time. Goods were lying here on Saturday which were billed from Grenfel to Indian Head, both stations east of here.
The week before last a car of United States immigrants was detained at Regina for three days as the company had not a spare engine to haul their coach and several cars of horses,
cattle and household effects north, every available locomotive being utilized to transport the Barr party to Saskatoon.
The Qu'Appelle ' Progress ' interviewed a number of representative business men recently and published their statements which show that a period of three weeks in transit was the very best time made between Winnipeg and Qu'Appelle, a distance of 324 miles, while in the majority of cases a month and one is recorded of goods shipped from Winnipeg on December 1, 1902, which were not yet to hand April 15, 1903. On this date also goods shipped from Montreal on February 27th, from Hamilton on March 10th, from Galt on March 14th had not arrived. The ' Progress ' states that 'more than one merchant is ready to show that he has lost hundreds of dollars by delay in delivery of goods.' Newspapers all over the North-west record the same state of things.
Of course, this is not at all a new story. We from the west had to complain last year of a most serious congestion of traffic which had existed then for several months.
I may say that the Canadian Pacific Railway is the only road the people of the North-west Territories know, and the only road they do business with.
