We were promised last year by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that any inconvenience we had suffered in the preceding season would not be repeated, but we found last fall that conditions were even worse than they were the year before. The Winnipeg board of trade, as everybody here is aware, is a very representative and intelligent body of business men, representing, as the lion, member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) sometimes points out, not only the people of Winnipeg, but, in some sense, the people of Manitoba and of the North-west Territories.
: That board of trade was led to frame a reso-, lution, and a stronger indictment of any I corporation or body was never framed than this resolution of the Winnipeg board of , trade, which l am going to place before the 1 House. It was not framed hastily. It was 1 discussed by the members of the board of ; trade on two, if not on more occasions. The 1 first proposition which was placed before 1 them in the way of a resolution was amend: ed and changed. This resolution was adopted after full and serious consideration, i and it goes on this wise :
Whereas, in the autumn and early winter of i 1901, the farmers and business classes of Mani-; toba and the North-west Territories suffered d severe losses through the inability of the Cana. dian Pacific Railway Company to cope with the i grain traffic ; and whereas, it was promised, on - behalf of that corporation, that it would sup-i ply itself with an equipment that would enable ; It to carry out the crop of the present year e (1902), and whereas, the company was authorized by parliament to issue additional stock to e the amount of $20,000,000, with the express con- dition that the proceeds were mainly to be used to purchase the necessary equipment, and s whereas, the conditions id regard to grain e transportation during the present shipping sea-o son are as bad as, if not worse, than those i, which prevailed in 1901, with the same result

of heavy 'loss to the farmers and to the community as a whole, and whereas, on account of the same lack of proper equipment, the railways have not been able to supply transportation for fuel, and as a result of their failure, great loss and much personal hardship and suffering have been experienced in nearly every portion of western Canada ;

These are weighty words if they are true, and I can assure the House that they are only too true.
-and whereas, the passenger service has become so irregular, unreliable and apparently disorganized, that much loss has been inflicted on business men, and the travelling public has suffered great and long-continued inconvenience and hardship, and whereas, the equipment of the railway company has fallen into such a condition that the corporation is utterly unable to handle the traffic of western Canada, and whereas, the people of western Canada, seem, under present circumstances, to have no recourse or redress against the corporation for the enormous losses which they have sustained, and whereas, the railway corporations have received from the parliament of Canada valuable franchises, monopolies and privileges, besides enormous donations of public money, grants of public lands and the use of the public credit for large sums, in consideration of the corporations providing an adequate and efficient system of public transportation ; and whereas, the parliament of Canada, as the charter-granting power, is the supreme and responsible authority in all questions relating to the regulation or control of public transportation, and the government of Canada is vested with authority to enforce the terms of charter obligations ;
Therefore, be it resolved : That this board respectfully urges the Dominion government to take such immediate action as shall remove the grievous disabilities under which the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories labour ; and to take such further measures as shall effectually prevent the recurrence of conditions such as those herein described ; that a copy of this resolution be transmitted by the secretary to the government of Canada, and to the Canadian Pacific Railway.
The Winnipeg board of trade found it necessary very recently to further consider this matter, and we see by the press reports that they have decided to send a delegation of their members to Montreal to personally interview the president and other head officials of the Canadian Pacffic Railway Company. I have one other document, and only one other, which I will ask the House to bear with me in reading, framed and adopted by the North-west Assembly in the shape of an address to the Governor General in Council. It goes on to say :
We, His Majesty's dutiable and loyal subjects, the legislative assembly of the Northwest Territories of Canada, in session assembled, humbly approach Your Excellency for the purpose of representing-
That after making due allowance for the extraordinary circumstances with which the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has had to contend it appears to this House-
That the practically continuous freight congestion of the last two years has abundantly Mr. SCOTT.
demonstrated that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company has absolutely failed to provide adequate facilities for the transportation of the grain, cattle and other natural products of these territories and that there has resulted in consequence of the lack of such facilities great loss and damage to the people of these territories not only in respect of the depreciation in the market price of grain but also in respect of cattle, and has further resulted in vexatious delays in the importation of merchandise and in the transaction of the ordinary business of the country :
That the volume of business originating along the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and in the territory directly tributary thereto necessitates that the energies of the company should be concentrated on the providing of adequate facilities for handling such business (which are not now provided) and that good faith with the people of these territories demands that branch lines already promised and partially constructed should be completed this year rather than lines in territory already provided with railway facilities, and
That the prospective increase in the volume of traffic which largely increased cultivation and settlement of lands in these territories will certainly create, will further tend to congest traffic between these territories and the provinces to the east, and unless it is held desirable to divert part of such traffic through foreign channels, adequate facilities for its transportation must be immediately provided, and
That this House does therefore humbly pray that Your Excellency may be pleased to take such action as may be necessary or expedient to insure that the people of these territories are provided with an efficient transportation system as contemplated by the contract made beween the people of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.
Now I may be asked and I very likely will be asked : Wliat are you going to do about it, or what can you suggest to be done about it ? I do not know that I should be held responsible for suggesting a remedy but at all events I do intend to suggest some course of action to the government which may result in bringing about a remedy. I wish to point out to the House that there are two distinct phases of the transportation question as affecting the people of western Canada at this moment. One has reference to providing immediate extension of lines, chiefly in the North-west Territories. The province of Manitoba is already fairly provided with railways so far as the mileage is concerned, but there is necessity in the North-west Territories for a very considerable and a very immediate extension of the railway mileage, because to-day the class of settlement that needs free homesteads has been forced long distances away from the existing railway lines. Even last year it was stated in the Railway Committee here that immigrants from the United States were being forced as far back as seventy-five miles from the Calgary and Edmonton Railway in order to obtain free homesteads, and a large number of the Barr colonists are at present going 180 miles away from any existing railroad. It is

plain that it is absolutely impossible for people to make a satisfactory living out of agriculture if they are located anything like that distance from a line of railway. It is computed that if a farmer is twenty miles away from a railway line he is at the extreme distance which enables him to make a satisfactory living. There is therefore necessity for the immediate extension of the railway mileage in the North-west Territories, but that is not the question which I intend to discuss this afternoon. The other phase of the question chiefly affects the people who live along the existing lines in the territories. The newspaper paragraph which I read has to do with those who live in towns, for instance the people of Regina, who have had the Canadian Pacific Railway for twenty years, and Regina is the southern terminus also of the Regina and Prince Albert line. The most urgent question now, is the question of furnishing facilities on the existing lines. It must be plain to the House that it is not a very sensible proposition to urge the extension of branch lines and other lines in that country, without first urging that provision should be made to facilitate the movement of traffic on the existing lines, because every mile of extension will mean more business and will consequently necessitate more facilities on the existing main roads, and more congestion if the facilities are not provided. I have here quite a mass of literature which is calculated to convince the House that this is an extraordinarily serious matter to the people of the North-west Territories. The blockade which has been most talked about for the past twenty months is the wheat blockade. That is uppermost in the minds of most people and it is perhaps the most serious, but it is not the whole difficulty by any means. I am neither a wheat grower nor a wheat dealer, but in my personal business I have experienced the effects of the traffic congestion in a way which leads me to speak of it with some feeling born of experience. An instance which occurred to me personally may appeal to the members of this House who are newspaper publishers. We in the western country buy practically all our paper supplies in eastern Canada, and I purchased some paper in the east about the first of March before I left Regina to attend the session. Under ordinary circumstances that paper should have reached Regina three weeks after, but as a matter of fact the office only received that paper last week, when it was fully five weeks overdue. But that is not the whole story. For three weeks I was receiving letters and telegrams constantly, advising me that the office was in very great difficulty on account of the nonarrival of this paper, and finally they told me that every stick of type in the office was set in form for the presses awaiting the arrival of the paper and that if some relief was not forthcoming the whole
staff would have to take a holiday. To relieve the difficulty I bought a quarter of a ton of type in Toronto, and as it was useless to put that type in a freight car, because there would be no guarantee that it would get there any time before Christmas, I sent the type by express. To alleviate my feelings I learned just after the type was sent by express, at very high charges, that the office was informed that the paper had been in the Regina yard for three weeks notwithstanding that inquiries were made to the railway agent at that point every day during these three weeks. That simply illustrates the extraordinary confusion which exists over the whole railway system in the west. The local officers of the railway are not at all to be blamed, because they are simply overworked, and have been overworked for months. They are not the men who are to blame. That is merely one instance which I cite as to my own personal loss. I will give another instance of the loss which was entailed on a Regina cattle shipper last fall. He ordered cars ten days ahead for the shipment of 250 export cattle, and he writes :
I had to hold my cattle here a week after the cars should have been here. The result was : I lost my buyer ; I lost the boat at Montreal ; and I was forced to take the shipment to Toronto. I fed at Winnipeg and again at Sehrei-ber, but the run was so slow, together with the six-inehes-deep mud pond in which the cattle had to lie down at Schreiber, that the animals fell off, looked badly and sold poorly. I lost a good thousand dollars by that week's delay in procuring cars.
It must be evident to every man in this House that such conditions will eventually prevent men from doing business in the west and will shake the confidence of the business community in our transportation system. To show the state of confusion that exists now, and which has existed for months, I will relate an incident that was given to me by a farmer of the Indian Head district, who told me that having shipped a car of wheat for Fort William, he waited the ordinary time, and not receiving returns he commenced to make inquiries, and after considerable delay he was informed that his car of wheat had been found at Lethbridge, which is six or seven hundred miles west of Indian Head, in place of at Fort William, which is six or seven hundred miles east. The Public Works Department of the government of the North-west Territories last year lost two cars of bridge timber which they had ordered in British Columbia, and after weeks of apparently fruitless search one of the cars which should have been at a point in southern Alberta was found down east of Estevan, in southern Assiniboia, and the other car was found north of Regina, but the timber which should have been on it was gone.
Hear, hear.

As every lion, gentleman here from the west knows, I might go on to give incident after incident of this kind, so that they would fill not only books but the whole library. These things go to show what the people of the west have been suffering for nearly two years. A worse phase of the matter than almost any I have spoken of is this, that from the early part of November till late in February, the people in Manitoba and in the greater part of the North-west Territories were on the ragged edge of a coal famine. If we had had last winter the kind of storms which we have suffered in some years, it is almost certain that hundreds of people in that country would have been frost-bitten, and that an absolute coal famine would have taken place. As it was, in certain parts of the country the farmers were driven to the necessity of burning their fences.
And their furniture.

My hon. friend from Saskatchewan says, ' And their furniture.' That was reported ; but I know that people were frequently deprived of coal because of the inability of the railway companies to deliver coal, and were driven to the necessity of getting fuel of other kinds. Then there was trouble in connection with the passenger service. Every department of the railway seemed to be short or disorganized. For five months at Regina the No. 1 express train from the Atlantic, heading for the Pacific, did not come into the place five times on schedule time. The trains were usually half a dozen hours late-sometimes three or four hours, sometimes five or six hours, occasionally twenty or thirty hours. The conditions would not have been complained of so bitterly if the people could have got any word of when they could reasonably expect the train. The train would be billed up an hour late ; passengers would go to the station at the specified time, and find that the detention was extended a couple of hours, and sometimes very much longer. The hon. member for Saskatchewan will remember one occasion in February, when he and I were at Maple Creek. No. 1 train, according to the schedule, should have passed there at half-past four o'clock ; but it was billed to arrive at eight o'clock. There were some parties there from Medicine Hat who wished to go home on that train. They sat in the hotel at Maple Creek till half-past eleven. The report came from the station that the train would certainly be in at a quarter to twelve. At a quarter to twelve the report came that it had not yet left Swift Current, and could not possibly reach Maple Creek till four o'clock. As a matter of fact, it came along at about five o'clock, and our Medicine Hat friends got on board to go home, after sitting the whole night in suspense. That kind of thing occurred during the whole winter. Conditions became so serious that the commercial travellers held
indignation meetings at Winnipeg and passed strong resolutions protesting to all concerned, as I am doing this afternoon, endeavouring to create some general realization of the conditions which the people in the country have to bear.
East year, when this matter of the Canadian Pacific Railway equipment was discussed, certain excuses were made by some members of the House for the company's lack of facilities, and I was myself disposed at that time to feel that there was some excuse for the company-that a swift rate of progress had come so suddenly on the country, and its growth was so fast, that it was not surprising that the company, like other people, had been taken somewhat unawares. But a year has passed since that time, and we find, contrary to the promises given by the company to the House and the country, that the conditions to-day are very much worse than they were then, and I think today the company is deprived of any reasonable or valid excuse for those conditions.
Occasionally an officer of the company will state in eastern Canada-he will not make the same statement in western Canada, because the conditions are too well understood there-that a great part of the cause of the congestion is to be found in the Manitoba Grain Act passed by this House. The company in that way tries to put the blame on the members of this House, implying that this House has passed a foolish and unreasonable Grain Act which has tied up the operations of the company. A reason of that kind would not stand very long if stated in the hearing of western people. The meaning of it is that the platform-loading provision of the Act holds the ears of the company, or is liable to hold them, for twenty-four hours. But that provision did not damage the power of the company last season one-half of one per cent, because during two or three months practically every siding on the whole system, in the Northwest Territories at all events-I am not so certain about Manitoba-was blocked with loaded cars, which, after being loaded with wheat, stood there week after week, in some instances as long as two months. That is sufficient to show that no weight at all is to be placed on the excuse of the company, that part of the reason of the congestion was to be found in the Grain Act.
We had it also stated to the House last year, and it is stated at odd times throughout the country, that it is unreasonable to expect that the company is going to move out the whole wheat crop during the navigation season, which is of about three mouths' duration. The people do not ask that ; but last year, out of a total crop of some 64,000,000 bushels, when navigation closed it was found that the Canadian Pacific Railway had only been able to haul to Fort William 15,000,000 bushels. So that when the company cannot haul 25 per cent of the crop in the navigation season, they

cannot contend that they have adequate equipment. I think every one now is compelled to admit that the conditions which prevail to-day and which have prevailed for the past twenty months, are due wholly and entirely to the lack of that equipment which the country has a right to expect the company to have, and which any company serving a district so important and in which the products promise to become so great, should have provided. But still we occasionally meet the statement that the business of that country has grown to such proportions that no single road could be expected to handle it.
I may say that in that statement I take no stock at all. I think it would be possible to have the present Canadian Pacific Railway line equipped in such a manner that it would not only do all the business to be done at present, but five or six times as much more to meet future demands. I am led to this belief by the conditions of other railways. On the Pennsylvania there are maintained twenty freight cars for each mile of track and that company has one locomotive in operation for every two miles of track. A proportionate equipment on the Canadian Pacific Railway would mean 160,000 freight cars and 4,000 locomotives. Last fall the Canadian Pacific Railway had only 27,000 freight cars and 743 locomotives. Hon. members may say that you cannot make a fair comparison between the Pennsylvania and the Canadian Pacific Railway. Then take a road with which a comparison may be more fairly made. Take the Northern Pacific. It has six cars per mile of track and one locomotive for every seven miles. That would mean 48,000 freight cars, as against 27,000 on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and 1,100 locomotives, as against 743. I have not here the actual figures regarding the equipment of the Great Northern, but I am informed that it moved in the month of November 12,000,000 bushels of grain, as against 15,000,000, which was all the Canadian Pacific Railway was able to move during the whole shipping season. And the Great Northern is a road which was built entirely, I believe, without public aid. Nevertheless it is equipped and operated as a private enterprise, and is running through a country which does not offer the business that our North-west does, so that there is all the more reason why the Canadian Pacific Railway should have far superior equipment. It may not be out of place to make some reference to the departments in which the Canadian Pacific Railway seem to be deficient. It is not a question of cars at all. I believe that last fall the company had sufficient cars for freight, if their other equipment had been up to the mark. I do not believe that it is a question of lack of locomotives so much as a lack In other departments. We know that last year the company put on ninety-eight new locomotives. and I believe that every new locomotive simply added to the congestion and 77
confusion. The deficiency seems to be in round-houses and shops more than locomotives. A gentleman who was here last week told me that he had seen at one time eleven locomotives in the Moosejaw yards, which had come in from their run in fairly good condition, and could not get into the shops, because the shops and roundhouse room were wholly inadequate. There may be sufficient shops in Winnipeg, but west of Winnipeg, at Brandon, Moosejaw and Medicine Hat and at other points, I am informed that the shops are simply what they were twenty years ago. Practically no increases have been made since the line was first built.
You cannot move grain with a round-house.

My hon. friend from South Essex says you cannot move grain with a round-house. Certainly not, but you must have locomotives, and you must keep them in order so that they may be able to move the grain, and to keep them in order, you must take them into the shops and have little repairs made to them. But owing to the impossibility of getting locomotives into the shops, they had to stand in the yard with water in them and the steam up and turn out again on their run, and the result was that all last fall and winter there were dead engines to be met everywhere. On one occasion the one locomotive on the Prince Albert branch died ; another was sent to its relief,' which, too died ; and finally there were five dead engines on the branch. Then there is a lack of sidings. In fact, in every department the equipment has become inefficient. The impression prevails amongst the people of the western country who pay attention to these matters- and most of us out there do-that for the sake of the stock market the Canadian Pacific Railway system has been simply starved for years. There is to be found the real reason for the existing condition. I have here a statement made about the Canadian Pacific Railway, as far back as 1S96, by a financial journal, so well known as the London ' Economist ' :
We cannot understand how the reduction of expenses referred to can possibly have been attained except by the postponement of necessary outlays. Expenses must have been cut down to the bone, and the future will have to afford a recompense.
In its succeeding issues, this paper criticised the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway and pointed out clearly what was bound to happen, almost as clearly as if at the time it had a knowledge of the facts existing to-day. The ' Economist ' pointed out that some day progress would come on the country with a rush and the company would be totally unable to keep up with it. No one in the west, who comes in touch at all with the railway officials, is ignorant of the fact that from year to year, or rather from



half-year to half-year-because, I understand, that the estimates of the road are made up half-yearly In many cases-the estimates sent down to the head office by the western officials were chopped sometimes sixty, seventy and eighty per cent, and the company have sometimes asked their staff on the western line to do the business with twenty per cent of the money which those officials declared necessary to keep up the system as it ought to be maintained.
I shall probably be asked what we are going to do about it. I do not know that I am very clear on that point in my own mind. Hut I am free to say that I think the problem is one which this government and parliament are bound to face and face boldly. Just what can be done, I do not know that I am prepared to say, but something must be done if Manitoba and the North-west Territories are not to receive a very serious check. There is one thing that may be suggested. In the Canadian Pacific Railway contract there are specific provisions with regard to the character of the service to be given by this company which was organized in 18S1. The company, of course, was placed under the general law with regard to the efficiency of service and that law contained these provisions. I am quoting from the statutes of 1879, the Consolidated Railway Act, section 25, subsection 2 :
The trains shall be started and run at regular hours to be fixed by public notice, and shall furnish sufficient accommodation for the transportation of all passengers and goods as are within a reasonable time previous thereto offered at the place of starting, and at the junctions of other railways and at usual stopping-places established for receiving and discharging way passengers and goods from the train.
3. Such passengers and goods shall be taken, transported and discharged at, from and to such places, on the due payment of the toll, freight or fare legally authorized therefor.
But, in the contract and in the Act of incorporation there are more stringent provisions. In section 3 of the Act by which the Canadian Pacific Railway contract was ratified, we find these sentences :
Upon the organization of the said company, and the deposit by them, with the government, of one million dollars in cash or securities approved by the government, for the purpose in the said contract provided, and in consideration of the completion and perpetual and efficient operation of the railway by the said company, as stipulated in the said contract, the government may grant to the company a subsidy

-and so on. Thus, it is very distinctly provided that there shall be efficient operation by the company in return for the valuable privileges and franchises conferred upon them. Also, under section 5 :
The Canadian Pacific Railway defined as aforesaid shall become and be thereafter the absolute property' of the company ; the whole, however, upon the terms and conditions,

-one of which I have recited

-and subject to the restrictions and limitations contained in the said contract.
There is a sentence at the end of section 7 of the contract:
And the company shall thereafter and for ever efficiently maintain, work and run the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I had already occupied more time than I had expected would be necessary in bringing the question of the serious congestion of railway traffic in the country to tiie attention of the House. But, possibly, if it is justifiable for lion, members to occupy a couple of hours discussing the question whether the officer commanding should or should not have made a particular speech, and to occupy fifteen of the twenty-eight-dollar minutes of the House in discussing whether a few yards of sod in front of these buildings should be taken out, it may not lie improper for an lion, member to spend some time in ventilating in the House such very serious conditions as do exist to-day, as inust be admitted to exist to-day, in this country with regard to railways.
Now, as I said before, I shall probably he asked : What do you suggest ; it is very well to talk about these conditions existing, but what are you going to do about it; what is it possible for this xiarliament to do ? Some hon. gentlemen may say that this is a business pertaining entirely to the company, that the company is responsible. But I think that when we remember the very large assistance that was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway by the people of Canada to assist at the inception of their undertaking, and the very considerable assistance that has been given to the company from time to time within the last twenty years, and when we consider the nature of the contract and undertaking the company entered into with the people of Canada, it cannot but be admitted that the representatives of the people in this parliament have a duty to perform, that they are face to face with that duty and are under obligation to deal with the problem without delay. We shall likely be told, also, that the company has already expended large sums of money. As a matter of fact, the information was given to the House yesterday, by the Minister of Railways (Hon. port wheat into the country elevators before the break up of the roads, which might be expected about the end of March, and before the seeding season came on, it was necessary that 13,000,000 bushels of wheat should be shipped out of the country-that would be between the 20th of January and some date towards the end of March. Mr. Whyte admitted that the largest amount his company could expect to handle within that time was 6,000,000 bushels. He said that they expected to be able to haul 3,000,000 bushels to St. John by rail, and they would, before the end of March, have an additional

The Territorial Commissioner of Agriculture, Mr. Bulyea, had just come from St. Paul where he had conferred with the officials of the Great Northern, the Northern Pacific and the St. Paul and Sault Ste. Marie roads; and he had come back to Regina with promises from these companies that they would accept all the wheat that the North-west could furnish to them within the next two months. They said there was at that time open space in the Duluth elevators for 30,000,000 bushels, and they had sufficient railway equipment at their disposal at the time to enable them to handle all the wheat that we could furnish to them. It was suggested, naturally, to Mr. Whyte that the solution of the problem as it existed then was that the Canadian Pacific Railway should turn over to the Soo and to the Great Northern the 7,000,000 bushels of excess. The House will scarcely believe me when I state that when this proposition was made to the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company he turned it down, he absolutely refused to allow the people of the North-west Territories to send out that excess of 7,000,000 bushels of wheat through American channels. When the question came up in that form the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway was intensely patriotic:	It would be acting against the interests of Canada to allow this wheat to go out over American roads, and rather than permit that, the wheat must lie upon the North-west farms and rot. It may be contended-if there is any one here to speak on behalf of the Canadian Pacific Railway- that I am putting the refusal of the president a little too bluntly. I may admit to you that when the fact was stated in the newspapers in the North-west Territories, the Canadian Pacific Railway did complain, and tried to hedge about their refusal. I may be permitted to read a letter which was sent with regard to this matter by Mr. Whyte, the assistant to the president. A newspaper in Regina had stated that Sir Thomas Shaughnessy had turned down the request of the Western Grain Growers' As-

sociation on that occasion, and Mr. Whyte sent this letter to the newspapers, dated January 31:
I am very much surprised at the article which appeared in your issue of January 29, headed ' The Canadian Pacific Railway refuses.' In fairness to the company I trust you will kindly publish this and my telegram to Mr. Bulyea, which I understand is the refusal you refer to, and which reads as follows :-
* I am authorized to say that instructions have been given to load back all cars coming in by the Soo line and Great Northern routes. Since our meeting '

That is the conference that I have referred to.
-' space has presented itself at Fort William by the opening of elevator D, and shipments to that point are being again accepted. Nearly 2,000,000 bushels more space will be available in March by the completion of new annex to elevator D at Fort William. Daily shipments are being made by our all rail route and we are taking all grain offered by that route as well as the grain for export that we can find ocean space for. Over 'two million bushels have been forwarded, all rail, since navigation. The company is fully alive to the requirements of the situation, and feels satisfied that the supply of cars now being sent to the territories will meet farmers' requirements.'
That is the kind of statement that has been repeated to the people of the west for many months, that the company was entirely satisfied that they were going to be able to meet all the requirements of the situation :
I may further add that during the last day or two cars supplied at stations in territories for use of farmers have not as yet been loaded and I will feel obliged if you can do anything to get them to load cars more promptly.
That was another characteristic and typical statement that we have had ever since the traffic congestion became apparent, and we have bad, month after month, the officials of the company endeavouring to put the blame on somebody else. Now this telegam of Mr. Whyte was just as much a refusal as the telegram of Sir Thomas Sbaugh-r.essy directed to the Commissioner of Agriculture had been, to the request that the company would permit a quantity of grain to be sent out over American roads, Mr. Sliauglinessy's reply was that the people who were in the conference-I suppose they must have included Mr. Whyte, the representatives of the Grain Growers' Association and the members of the North-west government-must have been unaware that the company was already allowing grain to be shipped out over American roads. The arrangement that was in force and to which the president referred was the arrangement that all American or foreign cars finding their way into the territories might be loaded and sent back over these roads. Prior to the 20th of January this arrangement bad been in force for over two months, and up to that time I venture

to say that not more than 40,000 bushels and in all probability not 25,000 bushels had then found their way out of the country. That arrangement might have been working for fifteen or twenty years before the
7,000,000 bushels requiring to be moved could have been sent out under it. The company repeated that they were quite satisfied that they would be able to deal with the situation. The House will remember that a year ago when we discussed the conditions that existed in the fall of 1001 the company professed to be quite satisfied that these conditions would never be repeated. It is such statements as these made by the company and which are never fulfilled that have led to a very serious intensity of feeling on the part of the people in regard to the operations of the company. I may say at the very time that Sir Thomas Shaughnessy patriotically was refusing to allow Canadian wheat to be hauled over American roads a number of grain dealers in Vancouver were obliged to refuse Australian orders for western Canadian wheat on account of the fact that the Canadian Pacific Railway was unable to deliver the wheat at Vancouver and the Australian dealers were obliged to go across the line to the state of Washington to get their orders filled. I must say, for my part, that when we find conditions like these and when we find an attitude like this on the part of the company the people of the west are entirely within their rights when they make representations to this government and to this parliament demanding that some action be taken on the part of the government and of parliament to compel the company to observe their charter and contract obligations. Before six o'clock I was referring to the very specific provisions which appear in the Canadian Pacific Railway contract. Defective as this contract is in many particulars in regard to the rights of the people it seems that the framers of it had been careful to have very specific provisions put in in regard to the character of the service which the company must maintain and I think I quoted before six o'clock from section seven of the contract. The last sentence of section seven states :
And the company shall thereafter and for ever efficiently maintain, work and run the Canadian Pacific Railway.
Section eight is as follows :
Upon the reception from the sovermnent of the possession of each of the respective portions of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the company shall equip the same in conformity with the standard herein established for the equipment of the sections thereby contracted for, and shall thereafter maintain and efficiently operate the same.
If a suggestion is demanded from me in the way of a remedy for the conditions of which I am complaining I will propose this : The company have plainly forfeited their charter rights by failing to give an efficient
service to the people of Canada in return for the very great privileges, franchises, subsidies and land grants that were handed over to them and if there is no other method of bringing the company to a realization of their responsibilities, or of compelling the company to carry out their charter obligations, I would suggest that a case be taken to the courts to decide now whether or not the suggestion I make is not the right one. Take a case to the courts and have a judicial decision given upon the point whether or not the Canadian Pacific railway have by their failure to serve the people forfeited their charter rights and whether these charter rights may not be taken away and such fresh arrangements made with the company by parliament as to the representatives of the people seem proper. There is another suggestion, perhaps a little less drastic than that, which may be made and which I think there is no doubt would very quickly bring an end to the condition of things against which we have at present to complain. In one section of the Manitoba Grain Act there are three words, which, if cut out, I think, would go a considerable length in very quickly bringing relief. These three words are ' without undue delay ' and they refer to the furnishing of cars. I think if we cut out these three words ' without undue delay ' a great deal of good will he done. I. make this suggestion to the government in all seriousness as a remedy for the conditions that are prevailing in the country at the present time. I propose to cut these words out of the Act and make the company liable to penalties for failure to give cars within a reasonable time after they are applied for, to put them under a penalty for failure to do the business of the country iu au efficient manner and I think that possibly next year and for all time to come we will not be under the necessity of taking up the time of the House iu making such serious complaints as I am endeavouring to voice at the present time. As I have said the position now has become entirely intolerable. This difficulty commenced about twenty months ago during the autumn of 1901 and the company told the people from time to time: Well, we have been caught a little bit but this will never occur again. We are going to make provisions which will remedy this condition next? season and there will be nothing like this to complain of. Well, next season came and we found that notwithstanding tlie great promises the company were making about the expenditure of money and the additional equipment and facilities they were providing-I say we found that last season, in the month of November, notwithstanding the promised additional equipment, that the company hauled 1,000 cars less to Fort William than they did the year before and that during the whole season of 1902 their haulage to Fort William was 750 cars less than their

haulage of 1901. I am bound to say that the cars were larger and that they hauled a few bushels more of wheat than in 1901, but as a matter of fact they hauled 750 cars less than during the preceding season. From time to time during the whole of last summer when it was apparent to almost everybody in that country who took the trouble to look into the situation that there was going to be a repetition of the blockade, business men, grain shippers, and others urged upon the company that they ought to bestir themselves and make some further efforts with the view of meeting the situation and the answer of the officers of the company was : What do you know about this matter ? Have you the information ? We have the information, we know what is being done and you do not know anything about it. We know ail about the conditions and we are perfectly satisfied that we can do all the business that requires to be done this fall. Yet, we find that the conditions were very much more serious than they were the year before. The same thing occurred during last winter at the time of this conference with Mr. Whyte. I was present at this conference at Regina on the twentieth of January when it was urged upon Mr. Whyte that not only in the interest of the company but in the interest of the country and the people generally the company should be only too glad to get rid of this 7,000,000 bushels of wheat because it was plain to every person that there was going to be an enormous immigration, that it would be necessary to haul down an enormous quantity of lumber and that in these ways the business of the company was going to be so greatly increased as to seriously tax the equipment of the company no matter how good it was and no matter how many additions were made to it.
But the officers of the company said: Oh, we are perfectly satisfied that we are going to be able to do the business all right. And the result is that the congestion and confusion at all points of the Canadian Pacific Railway, west of Winnipeg, are worse today than they ever were in the history of the country or in the history of the company. The Canadian Pacific Railway are perfectly satisfied; they were perfectly satisfied last fall when some of the settlers had to burn their fences because of lack of fuel. Of course the Canadian Pacific Railway tried to put the blame on other people; they do that constantly. There was a considerable amount of correspondence published in the newspapers late in the fall between the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the officers of the coal companies at Roche Percee and Lethbridge. The coal companies did not relish the idea of the Canadian Pacific Railway putting the blame for the fuel famine on them, and the officers of the coal companies made it clear to the officers of the railway company that the Mr. SCOTT.
latter were to blame for the condition of things that existed. Now, Mr. Speaker, I have not told one-thousandth part of all that might be told, but I think possibly l have occupied the attention of the House long enough and there are other representatives from the west who are prepared to supplement the few things that I have said. I emphasize the fact that this is not a local question, but that it is a national question. Probably the people west of Lake Superior feel the pinch more than others do, but there is no person in the Dominion who is not interested or who ought not to be interested in this question. There was a loss to the half a million people in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories, and that means a loss to all the people of Canada. I am convinced that there was a loss of not less than $10,000,000 last year to the people of the Northwest because of the conditions that prevailed on the railways. There was a loss of $5,000,000 on the wheat alone. I believe that the price of wheat was depressed an average of ten cents a bushel. I know of a particular case where the difference between what they call the ' street ' price and the 'track' price was as much as seventeen cents a bushel. That is to say, that when a farmer did procure a car by chance and was able to send out his own wheat and sell it, he got seventeen cents a bushel more for it than he was offered at the elevator. The House will recognize that auv condition which depresses the price of the farmer's wheat to the extent of ten cents a bushel, and seventeen cents a bushel in an extreme case, is an intolerable condition. I believe that the farmers of that country were robbed of not less than $5,000,000 on their wheat because of the condition that prevailed last year on the railway. In other ways, some of which I have described, there was a further loss, and I believe, Sir, that the people of that country were robbed of not less than $10,000,000 on the whole last year, because of this condition of things. The company tell us that they are not able to get the equipment, but I very much doubt that. They have been bonused and assisted enough by the people of Canada to warrant them in making an extra effort to save the people of the west from being robbed in the way I have described, and they could well afford to take say $3,000,000 to go to the markets of the world and purchase locomotives. I think that if I were furnished with $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 and let loose in Europe or the United States to pick up locomotives and freight cars I would not come back empty handed. Months ago I suggested, and I repeat the suggestion now, that a commission should be appointed by the government to study the conditions on that railway, and if necessary the1 commission should go to other countries to discover whether railway equipment cannot be bought with money, no matter what the price would be. It would pay the govern-

meat, if the company cannot stand the cost, to spend half a million or a million if necessary rather than to have half a million of the citizens of Canada robbed to tne extent I have stated. This is a phase of the question distinct from that of the extension of railway mileage in the west, and it js a phase which is of more immediate importance to us. It is absolutely useless to allow people to come to our country at the rate they are coming in now-35,000 new settlers up to the present this year, 20,000 during April alone-and to increase the production, if we do not take steps to see that their products can be shipped out. Every additional mile of railway built u Manitoba or the North-west Territories is merely going to add to the congestion if we do not provide facilities for operating the existing lines and accommodating the people in that country at the present time. The building of new lines of railway will not relieve this congestion in the time in which it must be relieved. It is impossible to build a new railway from the east to Winnipeg this year, and the unfortunate condition of things' I have described must be relieved this year if a worse condition is not to be created. Mr. Speaker, I trust I can with confidence leave this matter in the hands of the government and of the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext: Let me say a word or two on behalf of those people in Canada who have an interest in a land which is not North-west land. We fully recognize the importance of the west. As I have said on many occasions, we from the other provinces will be always glad; to do anything possible to promote the progress and development of our North-west lands, but we believe that the part of the country in which we live is just as good as the North-west, and that the half million people who are in Manitoba and the Territories are not any better people than we are. They are just as good but no better. We wish them God speed, but on our side we would like to have from them the right to be allowed to live. My hon. friend (Mr. Scott) has used very strong language indeed. He goes to the extent of saying that the people of Canada are allowing the Canadian Pacific Railway to rob the people of the west,
Hear, hear.

These are very strong words, but we have been hearing them in this House for the last three or four years. We are now told that this year the people of the west have been robbed of ten cents, or perhaps seventeen cents per bushel on their wheat. That is a statement for which I would like corroboration in stronger evidence than words. I do not believe that anything of the kind has happened and I do not think that my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) can prove it. He thought, of course, that he was speaking Gospel truth ; but he cannot prove what he has said. There has been congestion of trade in the Canadian west, just as there has been in the American west. The Northern Pacific and the Great Northern have not given better accommodation to the American farmers than the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern have given to our farmers. For two months the Great Northern could not handle its trade.
May I remind my hon. friend that I stated that in the month of January the Great Northern was able to handle all the grain the North-west Territories could give it.	.
There was just as much congestion on the American side as on the Canadian side.
There was congestion, but not much.

There was quite as much. Their roads could not take any more freight just then. If five additional railways were built in the Northwest Territories they could not possibly handle the trade during the season of navigation. The west is developing. Last year the season for moving the crop began on the 12th of October, none of the crop was moved before the 12th of October, and the Cth of December was the last day on which the port at Fort William was open. It was a very short season indeed. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian Northern, powerful as they are., cannot lengthen the season, and the government cannot do it either. Even if there were three or four more railways, they could not handle the trade of the west in such a short season. It cannot be done ; it is out of the question. My hon. friend has said that in the month of January an application was made to ship to Duluth 6,000,000 bushels of grain. Well, I doubt very much if there were 6,000,000 bushels of grain ready to be shipped at that time, and the hon. gentleman cannot prove it.
There were 14,000,000 bushels ready to be shipped.
The point is not whether the wheat was there. The question is whether the farmers were ready to ship it.
At the moment there were far more than 6,000,000 bushels of wheat in the country elevators.

I do not say that the grain was not there. What I say is that the farmers were not then anxious to ship their grain to that extent. The farmers were told that on application they would be given as many cars as could be placed at their disposal. Since the month of January the Canadian Pacific Railway has taken 3,000,000 bushels of grain on its all-rail route.

244S
Now, this country must stand by itself. There is a North-west, but there are also Canadian railways and Canadian ports; and the ambition of the Canadian people, when they decided to spend about $100,000,000 in building a great transcontinental railway, was to use their summer and winter ports as much as they could. Therefore the Canadian Pacific Railway is not only justified, but must make it a duty, to ship through Canadian ports all the trade they can handle. There are very many business men in this House, and there is not one of them who does not know that on many occasions he could not get immediately all the accommodation he wanted. There is not one shipper in the older provinces who, during the last two or three years, the last year especially, has not been obliged to wait for cars. I have seen on the sidings between Montreal and western points last year as many as 1,500 cars waiting. We could not ship everything at the same time. Our friends in the west must submit to the inevitable, as we have to do in the older provinces. My hon. friend, who is generally moderate in his views, has not been very mild to-day, but has gone to extremes. He has given us as an evidence of bad management and bad will on the part of the Canadian Pacific Railway the fact that one car has been lost track of. Well, among the many thousand cars that are moved on a great railway, it is not a miracle that one car is lost. I remember very well, during my travels on the other side of the ocean, that one of my friends lost his wife for two long days ; but he found her all right- she had been in good hands. Joking apart, it seems to me that our lion, friends from the west, instead of doing their level best to depreciate a great Canadian enterprise, would be wiser to join with us in finding the best means of alleviating the situation. What is the use of giving delight to the, great American railways, the competitors of the Canadian Pacific Railway ?-because that is what it means. Every blow aimed at this great enterprise gives delight to its American competitors. It seems to me that we should stand by each other better than our friends from the west do. Let them permit me to say that to them in all friendliness : They are wrong in their views, and in the policy they are pursuing.
My hon. friend has admitted that the Canadian Pacific Railway has spent about $7,000,000 in equipment. That is a large sum. Why, the port of Montreal, needs today an expenditure of $5,000,000 or $6,000,000. The older provinces have some importance, but we do not get up in arms and say that we are not getting anything. We understand that we must move with the times and take into account the difficulties we have to meet. As far as I am concerned-and I know that I am expressing the feelings of the great majority of this parliament-we will stand for Canadian Hon. Mr. TARTE.
ports as against American ports ; and if our friends from the west have to wait a little, they will have to hold their souls in patience as we are doing. The two railways already in that country have equipped themselves to the best of their ability. My hon. friends know that the Canadian Pacific Railway have tried to get more stock than they have been able to secure. They have given orders to some Canadian corporations for locomotives and they are not yet delivered, with the view of encouraging Canadian industry. They have applied to the United States, France, England and Germany for cars and locomotives, but could not get them for love or money. My hon. friends from the west cannot be ignorant of that. What is the use then of getting up in the House and saying that the Canadian Pacific Railway are robbing the people of the west to such an extent that their charter should be forfeited ? That is going very far in the wrong direction.
There is another fact which my hon. friend knows perhaps better than any body else. Water supply for the locomotives was not available. In the grain growing districts during the months of August and September and October, in the season of 1900, the rain fall was 7-66 inches, the following year it was 4'37 and last year it was only 2-31 inches. The result of that was that not sixty per cent of the power of the locomotives could be used. My hon. friend knows that as well as I do, and probably better because he was there.
There was a lack of expenditure to provide the water.

There was no rain and therefore that was the fault of the Canadian Pacific Railway. That is just the way we are treated, I do not believe that it is fair for us members of parliament, even members representing such a large portion of Canada as the North-west, to take such a stand. It may be if the Canadian Pacific Railway had foreseen that there would be no rain, they would have dug new wells. I do not know what kind of work should be done there to secure water, but all the same the supply of water was not available because the Divine Providence did not send sufficient rain.
Mr. SCOTT, alight I ask my hon. friend what weather statistics he is quoting from, because, as a matter of fact, every one in the North-west knows that last year we had a good deal more rain than the year before.
An hon. aiEaiBER. It swept away the bridges.
Hon. air. TARTE. aiy hon. friend says that there was so much water that the bridges were carried away. They were carried away in the month of June, but not in the months of August, September and October. That is just the kind of argu-

ments these lion, gentlemen use. If my hon. friends will permit me, I would tell them that that sort of thing appeals to prejudice and nothing else.
I was in Calgary in the middle of July and was held up there for three days by high water.

We know now that it rained in July, but is that evidence that it rained in August, September and October. What I say is this, and the truth of my statements can be easily ascertained, that in the months of August, September and October of last year, there were only 2 31 inches of rain. That is my statement and it is true. My hon. friend knows that most of the locomotives were nearly half the time in the shops because the water became so bad that it was thick.
They did not have room in the shops for them.
They had not any shops to put them in.

There is no arguing with those who do not wish to use arguments. There was no water. It is a well known fact, which my hon. friends know as well as I, that the locomotives could not work because of lack of water. But at the end of the speech of my hon. friend, we found the real reason for his utterances. He says : we want new lines. The Canadian Pacific Bailway has already spent between $7,000,000 and $10,000,000 for equipment, for locomotives, for cars, for sidings and for other works, but that is not enough because we must have new lines. In other words, the Canadian people are being given notice to-day that an application for $7,000,000, $10,000,000, perhaps $15,000,000, will be on the Table in a short time. That is the meaning of the speech we have just heard. The policy of the government is not yet known, but I believe that fair notice of motion has been given us to-night. We have a large surplus in the treasury, business is booming, applications are booming also-applications from the different provinces for larger subsidies, applications from the North-west for perhaps $10,000,000. It is fine, it is interesting, but all the same I cannot forget-we from the older provinces cannot forget-that there are other needs, that we cannot comply with every demand from every part of the country-from every Tom, Dick and Harry-but we must think of ourselves a little, and I invite the attention of the House and the country to the statements made here to-night. We have been given notice of motion that an application for further subsidies for a large amount of money will be on the Table before long. We will discuss them when they come before us. But in the meantime it is but fair to state that both the Great Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Bailway have, during the last year, added a
vast amount to their rolling stock and drawing capacity. Thousands of cars have been added to the rolling stock of the Canadian Pacific Bailway since the last season. The elevator capacity along the line of the Canadian Pacific Bailway has been increased by 7,500,000 bushels. At Fort William and Port Arthur alone, the additional elevator capacity for the season will be 4,000,000 bushels. The Canadian Northern has done a great deal also. I had the pleasure of travelling over that road last fall. The road was not in just as good shape as now, but the company have done very fine work indeed. They a're adding to their branches and the efficiency of their road. My hon. friend has, perhaps, lost sight of the fact that, if more grain was not taken from Manitoba and the North-west during navigation season, it is for the reason-besides the one I have already given-that there was a shortage of ships. At the close of navigation, there was a good deal more grain in store at Fort William than there was at the close of the previous season.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) should not say so, because he will be giving comfort to the American shipowners-using the same argument as he used about the Canadian Pacific Bailway.

The comfort of the American ship-owners does not concern me. We are discussing a question of fact; and I state again, as a matter of fact, that, when the season closed last fall, there was in the Canadian Pacific Bailway elevator at Fort William, more grain than there was at the close of the previous season.

I think'my hon. friend's (Hon. Mr. Tarte's) information is not quite accurate. There never was a moment in the last shipping season closing on the 5th of December, when the elevators at Fort William were blocked with wheat.
I did not say that.
That is the whole question.

No ; what I say is that ships could not be secured to take out the balance of the wheat in the elevators That cannot be denied. My hon. friends always try to avoid the issue. I did not say the elevators were blocked, but that more grain was left in them at the close of last season than at the close of the previous season, and that for the reason that no ships were available. And, in the month of April, before the opening of navigation, there was less grain in store by a million bushels than at the same time in the previous season. And why ? Because the Canadian Pacific Bailway have been carrying out grain by their all-rail route. Now, my hon. friend has said a word about the Grain Act. I would be very much surprised if my hon. friend would say front his place in this House that the Grain Act has worked to the satisfaction of the North-west farmers.

I say it.
lion. Mr. TARTE. May I be permitted to ask if it is not true that meetings have been held to denounce the Grain Act and ask for changes ?
No.

Yes, there was a meeting at Brandon. Will my hon. friend say there was not such a meeting to denounce the Act or ask for changes ? And I have been informed that, on several occasions, farmers have asked for a great many more cars than were necessary, thus keeping these cars idle-cars that might have been used elsewhere. Our friends from the North-west cannot possibly expect that the railway companies will ever be able to handle all their grain within the season of navigation. It would not be in the interest of the farmers themselves, for it would flood the market. But, aside from that, it is out of the question for a railway company to be able to handle a hundred million bushels of grain-still less two hundred million bushels, as we hope soon to have-within the season of navigation. What, then, is to be done ? Would it not be fair to expect that our friends in the west should do what their friends and neighbours in the United States have done-build granaries ? The farmers of Dakota and Minnesota have built granaries.
So have our farmers.
Only a few of them.
I can inform the hon. gentleman that there are four millions of bushels on the farms yet-in the granaries.
I speak of private granaries.
Yes.

There are granaries at the stations. But the farmers in the United States have built them on their own farms. In the older provinces we have done the same. Our friends in the west want us to give all the money that may be made available for them, but they do not want to help themselves even to the extent of building private granaries on their own farms. They will make all the greater profit if they resort to the methods that the American farmers have adopted.
The railway company must carry lumber to the farmers before they can build granaries.

I know from past experience that if the Canadian Pacific Railway were to spend in the North-west Territories all the money they could raise on their credit, there would still be grumbling. We are not surprised at that. Our friends from the North-west are right in making known their grievances, if those grievances are legitimate. But when I hear a member of parliament, and a very intelligent one Hon. Mr. TARTE.
too, tell us that one car has been lost and that the farmers of the west have been robbed of ten millions of dollars, I ask myself whether it "was not necessary to have a pretty large fund of patience not to get a little mad. Our friends in the North-west have not been robbed of ten millions of dollars. They have been subjected to the difficulties that other parts of the country have been subjected to. The farmers of the province of Quebec have not been able to ship all their hay at the same time. They well understood that they could not get all the accommodation they would like to have. But they have not instructed any of us to try to destroy the credit of great Canadian corporations. My hon. friend has spoken of the coal famine. I believe I am within the truth in saying that no part of the country has been better stocked with coal than our own Manitoba and the North-west. We have been short of coal in the older provinces. Where is the member of parliament who has not been short of coal this year ? We have been all short of coal. But we have not made it a grievance against heaven and all the railway corporations in the world. It has been an accident, an accident that our friends from the west should be ready to accept as we have done. Before taking my seat, I say again that, ready as we are to vote all the money that is necessary to develop the North-west, there is one thing that we will not lose sight of- that the North-west must be Canadian from a commercial standpoint. Now, when they ask us to give them all the money we can gather, and to allow them besides to ship their trade through American ports, they are going too far, the country will not support them. The country will stand by the Dominion in summer and in winter. The port of St. John and the port of Halifax should become more and more the winter shipping points of the country. We should have a definite and clear policy to that effect. This is hot the first time that I have protested against the policy that is too often propounded by some of our North-west friends. They look to Duluth, they look to Chicago.
What did we see during the last session of the local House ? Mr. Hill and his associates applied for charters granting them permission to build 2,500 miles of branch lines in Manitoba and the North-west Territories. Why did they do so ? I believe I know something of their reasons, I am not far astray when I say that they did so because they were encouraged by people who have not Canadian interests at heart, who have some other interests to serve. I believe I am telling what is the fact when I say that Mr. Hill succeeded because there has been an unholy agitation in the Northwest in favour of allowing Mr. Hill and his American associates to invade Canadian soil and Canadian territory, to tap the Canadian land so as to divert our trade through American ports. Mr. Roblin, who resisted

the year previous, was obliged to yield during the last session. A strong agitation was carried on by some of their friends and their organs, by the ' Free Press ' especially, the organ of an hon. gentleman on this side of the House, which resulted in forcing the hands of the legislature of Manitoba into giving permission to Mr. Hill and his associates to build 2,500 miles of railway so as to carry our Canadian trade to the American Great Northern and to the Northern Pacific, Mr. Hill's roads. I do not believe those lines will be built, I do not believe Mr. Hill will build those lines. The reason lie applied for charters was to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway Company from going any further into his field. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company have their Soo line, from which they are taking trade summer and winter to our Canadian ports, and Mr. Hill has found Canadians in the North-west who have helped him to check the Canadian Pacific Railway. That is just what has taken place. Sir, we are not friends of such an anti-Canadian policy as that. It is just as well that these things should be clearly stated in the House ; it is time to state the facts openly.
I think the question raised by my hon. friend is of vast importance. The blockade of grain is only one incident, there are larger questions behind, and one of them I have just alluded to a moment ago. Mr. Hill and his associates, I say it again, have been helped in their efforts to take possession of the charters of the North-west Territories and to force the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway from taking American trade to Canadian ports. I say that is an anti-Canadian policy. I say it is the duty of this parliament to stand by this country. Sir, X thank my hon. friend who has raised the question. He has shown us the efforts that are being made to-day by important interests, helped by public men in this country, to divert Canadian trade to American roads. History perhaps will.tell ns more than the past has told us. Perhaps the Canadian, nation will know more in the future than it has learned in the past. I^et us be careful, let us look carefully into the projects and schemes that may come before this parliament. Let us realize that our first duty is to stand by this country. Our electors, the people of Canada, will look to us to pro tect their best interests. The Canadian North-west will find friends in this parliament, as many friends as there are independent members, independent of railway corporations and financial interests. There are a great many members of parliament who are not influenced by such corporations. But the efforts that are being made to-day in certain quarters have to be watched with care. Our friends in the North-west may rely upon us, we will give them all the money that Is necessary to relieve them from the difficulties under which they labour
But the North-west must remain-I say it again with all the energy I can command- the North-west must remain Canadian. No Duluth, no Chicago for our business, but Montreal, Quebec, Three Rivers in summer-

May I ask the hon. gentleman just here, whether it is not a fact that the associations, accompanied by the Minister of Public Works, sought relief last October by going to Montreal first and discussing the question with the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and then sought relief from the American lines when they could get no satisfaction ?
Hon. Mi-. TARTE. My hon. friends came to the city of Montreal, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company gave them all the relief it could possibly give them. I do not speak so much of the past as I do of the future. I am looking towards the future, because when we see efforts put forth, one of which I have-just brought to the attention of the House, and when we see that such efforts have succeeded through the help that Mr. Hill and his associates have received from certain public men in this country, 1 say our duty is to be careful.
Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to say so much. But I think the time has come when the railway policy, the transportation policy of the country should be studied with more attention, and considered more carefully than it has been in the past. We are on the threshold of a new era. This country is developing by leaps and bounds. At last we are getting some immigration. We will get more if we stand by our country, if we equip it. We have all the money and all the credit that we need to do so. It takes a little time, governments cannot do everything in a day. The Canadian Pacific Railway and the Great Northern have done well in the past. The Grand Trunk Railway wants to build a new railway through the west ? We shall see how they want to build it. I know that this parliament would not consent to anything else than a thoroughly Canadian policy for the Grand Trunk Railway Company as for others, but we will discuss that later on. We do not know what the Grand Trunk Railway will tell us; we do not know whether they will apply for a subsidy or not. That will come later on. I only allude to that in passing and just to emphasize my view that this country is ready to do anything that our credit will permit us to do, but with this essential condition that the North-west Territories will stand with us. Our friends in the North-west Territories may just as well make up their minds now that they must look to the St. Lawrence route both summer and winter. If they ask us for millions to enable them to achieve that end they will get them. There will be no trouble as to that, but, if they ask us to sanction ahy I policy which will permit them to divert the trade of the North-west to American ports,

I think they will meet with a response that will surprise them.

Mr. Speaker, as one of the representatives in this House from the west referred to in no very complimentary terms by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreat'(Hon. Mr. Tarte) who has just taken his seat.'! want to inform the House and also the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, that the people who have representatives in this House expect that these representatives are going to look after their interests, and they have a perfect right on all occasions to get up and voice the sentiments of that part of the country from which they come without being called to account by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, or any person else. Now, I propose to say what I believe to be in the interests of the people of the North-west. It is true that I have not as large a brief as the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal. My brief is not typewritten ; it has not been prepared for me. I know that railways have a manner of reaching the House which the farmers have not except through their representatives. I am here as the advocate of the farmers. My brief is not so long as that of the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, but I will endeavour to deal with the situation as briefly as possible. I noticed that in the speech which the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, treated the House to, he dealt almost exclusively with the grain blockade. I want to draw his attention and the attention of the House to the fact that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) in discussing this matter this afternoon, spoke very briefly on the question of the grain blockade, that, in fact, he only devoted a few moments to it. The balance of his speech was directed towards other things, to the blockade of merchandise^ of cattle and a hundred and one other things, and as a matter of fact he scarcely touched upon the grain blockade at all, while the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, with his Railway Co. brief in hand dealt exclusively with the grain blockade, which went to show that his brief had been prepared beforehand and that it was a little old before he presented it to the House. He says that the people of the west are no better than the people of the east.' I do not think that any hon. member from the west has ever claimed that the people from the western territories and provinces are any better than the people from the east. We have never claimed that at all and we have never been unreasonable in our demands. If our people have grievances I think we have a perfect right to ventilate them as we see fit without being called to account by any person.
We do not deny that.

The hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, took exception to a state-Hon. Mr. TARTE.
ment made by the hon. member for West Assiniboia in reference to a certain amount of money that the hon. member for West Assiniboia said the farmers lost on their wheat. He went so far as to say that he had not any proof and that he did not know what he was talking about. I think the hon. member for West Assiniboia is in a much better position to deal with western questions and is much better versed in western questions than the hon. member for St. Marys, Montreal, is or will be in the near future. However, I am bound to say, he has travelled a great deal about the eastern provinces. We saw in the press about his trips on boats here and there and he went all over the country assuring the people that they ought to keep Canada for the Canadians, but he never came up to pay us a visit or to tell the people of the west that they ought to keep Canada for the Canadians. We know that without being told by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal. Now, he told us in his speech that the Great Northern Railway across the border was given no better service to the people over there than the Canadian Pacific Railway was given to the people of this country. I want to draw his attention and the attention of the House to the fact that last autumn the stock raisers of Alberta had to drive more than two-thirds of their whole product across the border to the Great Northern Railway lief ore they were enabled to market their stock. Thousands and thousands of Canadian cattle had to be driven across the line and shipped out over the Great Northern Railway in order to get to market.

The reason why the cattle were driven over the American line was this :	These shippers of cattle had
come to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and asked them to discriminate against the port of Montreal and in favour of the port of Boston. The Canadian Pacific Railway declined to do so while the Great Northern agreed to do so. The Canadian Pacific Railway declined to discriminate against the port of Montreal and then the people simply drove their cattle across the line. The Canadian Pacific Railway did the right thing then.

While not wishing to contradict the hon. gentleman as I said a short time ago in his speech he found fault with the hon. member for West Assiniboia for making the statement that the farmers of the west had lost a certain amount of money on account of the blockade and he said that he wanted the proof. In carrying out the same principle I would like to have proof of the statement which the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, has just treated this House to before I will be willing to take much stock in it.

The hon. gentleman knows that it is a public fact that the Cana-

dinn Pacific Railway were offered those cattle but they declined to discriminate against the port of Montreal.
