If the hon. gentleman says it is a fact it must be confined to the hon. gentleman and a few of his friends because I never heard of it before.
It has been stated in the press publicly.

I just wish to suggest to the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte), and also to the hon. member for Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) that the trouble in regard to the cattle, as I understand it, was that they could not get shipping from the port of Montreal.

No, they could get shipping. As soon as 1 read the statement in the press, I went myself, to the Canadian Pacific Railway offices in Montreal. The statement was made then in the 'Star,' 'Da Patrie ' and other newspapers on the authority of the Canadian Pacific Railway managers in Montreal and it is perfectly true that the Canadian Pacific Railway declined to discriminate against the port of Montreal and that then these cattle owners simply drove their* .cattle across the line to the Great Northern.

I remember a famous expression used by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, at one time that ' business is business.' I quite understand the cattle trade because I happen to be engaged in it and I know that if the Canadian Pacific Railway had not discriminated against the port of Montreal and that if they had fixed their rates right and given the same facilities for shipping and feeding and that sort of thing as were afforded on the other side of the line, the cattle owners of the country, who are as patriotic as any other class of people, would have sent every head of stock over the Canadian Pacific Railway to a Canadian port. It was the Canadian Pacific Railway who were not patriotic. It was not a case of Canada for the Canadians with them, but of keeping up high rates and not furnishing proper facilities for handling the stock. The result was that the cattle owners were obliged to drive their stock across the line and ship it by an American road.

My hon. friend has not understood me. These cattle owners wanted to ship their cattle to Boston and they wanted the same rate for Boston as for the port of Montreal and the Canadian Pacific Railway declined to grant it. That is all.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to tell me that the cattle shippers of the west would prefer shipping cattle from Boston rather than from Montreal, if they had not to pay a higher rate via Montreal ? Why the thing is nonsensical. If the cattle shipper of the west got the same facilities he would far rather ship from a Canadian than from an American port. But the truth
is that after driving the cattle something like 200 miles over the prairie they made a saving in time, and 83 per head in freight rates. If, besides, they had shipped them by the Canadian Pacific Railway the cattle would have depreciated at least one cent a pound, which is the difference between the price of export cattle and butchers' cattle. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) gets himself into deep water when he commences to talk about the Cattle trade, because he is not well posted on it. He had better get his brief amended. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) thought he had a point against my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. -Scott) when he stated that the time was too short to get our wheat out of that country before the close of navigation. What was he going to do with all the famous canals he was going to build to carry our wheat, if the season is so short that we could not ship by those canals, but would have to store our wheat at the head of the lakes all the time. We would like to hear something further from him on that aspect of his canal policy. The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Tarte) also told us that the people of the west would have to be treated in the same manner as the people of the east, that we were after money all the time. We have never asked for different treatment, and I can tell the hon. gentleman that if you look at the estimates for the last five years-throwing out the revotes, because he was great on revotes when he was Minister of Public Works-you will find that the western provinces did not receive their fair share of expenditure or fair treatment from the government so far as public improvements are concerned. The hon. gentleman also told us in his very dramatic fashion that every blow we struck at the Canadian Pacific Railway was helping the American roads. Not five minutes after he attacked the Canadian shipping interests by stating that they were not competent to take the wheat from Port Arthur and Fort William. If the people of the west are unpatriotic for striking blows at the Canadian Pacific Railway, he is unpatriotic when he strikes a blow at the Canadian shipping industry. But anyway the hon. gentleman had no argument in that. If the people of the west are labouring under a grievance from the Canadian Pacific Railway or any other railway corporation, does he mean to say that we have not the right to ventilate our grievances in this House, simply because that corporation howls that it is not patriotic for us to do so. If you carry that argument to its logical conclusion, you might as well say that if a Canadian robs a man, that man should keep his mouth shut about it simply because if he did not he would be holding up a Canadian a thief before the American people.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I have a good word to say for the Canadian Pacific Railway.

The Canadian Pacific Railway is a good company in some respects, and they have done a great deal for this country, but at the same time this country has done a great deal for the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think we are pretty even in that respect. The Canadian Pacific Railway entered into an agreement with the people of Canada by which on their side they received a certain amount of constructed road, a certain amount of public lands, a certain amount of public money, and certain other concessions in the way of exemptions for ever from taxation on their main line and buildings; certain exemptions from taxation on their lands for twenty years, as we supposed, but which we find out to be forty years ; and on top of all that they got the right to tax the people to their hearts content in the way of freight rates, and there is no question but that the Canadian Pacific Railway does that. In consideration of all this they were to give a fair and proper service to the people of Canada, west and east. The Canadian Pacific Railway should be compelled to carry out their agreement. The people of Canada have loyally carried out their part of the agreement. The poor settlers in the west who by their labour increase the value of their own lands were increasing the value of the Canadian Pacific Railway lands at the same time, and they made it possible for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to realize something like $100,000,000 out of Canadian Pacific Railway lands. The farmers of the Northwest felt very sore over the grievances which they laboured under at the hands of the Canadian Pacific Railway in this matter of taxation but when it was made known to them that there was a solemn agreement entered into between the people of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway, they loyally decided that they would labour under their disabilities in order to carry out their contract. But, Sir, on the other hand the Canadian Pacific Railway should be forced to carry out their share of the bargain just as loyally. Now, Sir, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) was not far astray in his figures when he spoke of the amount of money that the people of the west have lost on account of the conditions that have existed in that country last year. There were about 25,000,000 bushels of wheat shipped out of that country last year, and I am here to say that through the inability of the Canadian Pacific Railway to handle that traffic the farmers lost not'less than five or six cents a bushel, and any gentleman can take a pencil and figure out what that means. It means a loss to our farmers of $1,250,000. The buyers had to buy the grain early in the season on the basis of winter storage, because they had no guarantee that the wheat could be shipped out on account of the scarcity of cars and motive power. When a farmer happened to get a car and was able to ship his wheat

to the lakes, he got six cents a bushel more than the grain buyer could give him at his own door. The farmers commenced to complain that the grain buyers were robbing them, but the whole thing came back to the fact that the biggest railway in that part of the country was not able to handle the traffic offered to them. There are about
14,000,000 bushels of wheat yet in the country that the railway was not able to take out, and on every bushel of that the farmer will lose six cents a bushel or $840,000. They have to pay insurance, storage, and interest on the money, because the farmers are like other business people and if their product is not marketed they have to borrow money to pay interest on it, and interest is eight or ten per cent in the west. But it is not only the farmers who have lost. The business men all through the North-west have lost money by reason of the inability of the Canadian Pacific Railway to bring in freight. That loss ultimately comes out of he settlers. My hon. friend (Mr. Scott) gave a case where the Christmas goods ordered by a merchant did not arrive until the spring. And any business man knows that you cannot sell dolls and jumping jacks in the spring of the year unless you are willing to take five cents on the dollar for them. The hon. gentleman from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) does not appear to know as much about the cattle industry as he does about the wharfs and piers in this part of the country, and I want to give him a little information about that industry.
There are two classes of cattle which we have to ship. One class is known as export cattle; they are worth in Winnipeg from $4 to $4.15 per 100 pounds. The other class is known as butchers' cattle, which are worth at Winnipeg three cents per pound. On a $1,400 pound steer, the difference in price amounts to a considerable sum. Just $14 again out of the farmer. When a cattle shipper wants to ship his cattle from Calgary, he may find when he gets to Moose-jaw, a divisional point, that there is no accommodation. If another shipper has got ahead of him, there is no shed, no yard, no hay, no water, for his cattle ; so they have to go on. I have known of cattle to be three days on the cars without food or drink, and every one knows what that means. It means a reduction of 1T5 cents per pound on half of these cattle at least, because while half of them may be able to stand the hardship, the other half will go to pieces, and will have to be sold as butchers' cattle. That very thing happened all last fall. I had an experience of that kind myself. It took me one night and a whole day to go ninety-five miles with my cattle on the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I arrived at a place where I had to feed them, but there was no yard and no hay, and I had to break the Sabbath in order to go and hunt a yard and provide water and feed for my cattle ; and when

I got them: to the market I lost 1T5 cents per pound on half of them. Is it any wonder that people will take their cattle to the Great Northern, which provides them with yard and shed accommodation, and with the food and water they require ? It will take a great deal of patriotic talk to induce a man to go through rain and shine with his cattle, to go without proper accommodation, and to be willing to take a ceut per pound less for them in order to send them by the Canadian Pacific Railway. Let the Canadian Pacific Railway be sufficiently patriotic to give the people the facilities they require, so that they will be able to use Canadian roads and Canadian ports.
May I ask, are there several stations where there is not accommodation ?

Yes, several stations.
I-Ion. Mr. TARTE. How many ?

If my hon. friend will ask the Canadian Pacific Railway company (whose brief he holds), they will tell him all about it. Now, I have been looking over a very important and good report, in which there is a great deal of information ; and I hope my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) will not accuse me of being unpatriotic because I quote it in the House. That is the report of the Interstate Commerce Commission for 1901. At page fifty-one of that report I find that for every thousand miles of railway in the United States, taking the average all over the country, there were 195 locomotives and 7,535 cars. If my hon. friend will figure up the whole system of the Canadian Pacific Railway, he will find that it falls very short of that. There is no good reason why it should not have locomotives. This is not a new idea; it has been brought up here year after year. I have been in this House seven years, and every year during that time this House has been told that there were not sufficient facilities on that railway. The company have had plenty of time to remedy this state of affairs, and they should have done so. I also find that of the capital stock invested in railways in the United States, no less than 54-34 per cent paid no dividends in 1901, while the Canadian Pacific Railway has been paying five per cent and six per cent on its different classes of stock, though it has immense stretches that are unprofitable. All this bears out the statement of the hon. member for Western Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) that the company have been starving the road from year to year. If they had been putting the money earned by the road into improvements instead of into the stockholders' pockets as dividends, we would not have to make these complaints. My hon. friend from St. Mary's spoke of water tanks, and he said the rainfall in June had not been sufficient to keep them supplied. When he was called up by the hon. member for
Assiniboia, he dropped from June to July, and if my hon. friend had followed him up, he would have made him drop down to December. In the country we had a succession of dry seasons when there was very little water ; but during these years we never heard a complaint of shortage of water on the Canadian Pacific Railway, but now there is a complaint of shortage of water when the seasons are so wet that it is hardly possible for people to travel across the country and bridges were swept out in all directions by too much water caused by excessive rainfall. The simple fact is that the tanks have been neglected and the locomotives have been worn out. I might give my hon. friend an example of how the business has been done. In my own town of Prince Albert there is a branch line called Qu'Appelle, Long Lake and Saskatchewan Railway, which has been operated for twelve years by the Canadian Pacific Railway. There is a river as large as the Ottawa river, flowing past the town of Prince Albert, and the railway track runs within less than a hundred feet of that river ; and yet the company can get no water at Prince Albert, and have to take the locomotives out twenty miles to get water.

Will my hon. friend allow me ? Is it not a fact that about sixty per cent of the locomotive power of the Canadian Pacific Railway-new locomotives- have been out of shape during the months of September and October because of the alkali in the water, the result of there being no rain ? I have been informed that that is the case.

There is a certain amount of truth contained in the question the hon. gentleman asks. But the difficulty was this, that the company failed to make provision for good water at points like Prince Albert, where they have the Saskatchewan, which is free from alkali. At that point there should be no difficulty getting water, but they have failed to make provision to keep up their supply. At Regina also, where the water from the wells is too hard for proper service in the locomotives, they have failed to make provision for getting good water, but they are making it now. The offices of the company are filled with reports made by the company's officials with regard to this particular matter-reports made seven and eight years ago but only acted on this year. Had these recommendations been acted on years ago, there would not have been any difficulty.

I have in my hand a report from an official of the Canadian Pacific Railway to the effect that owing to the rain fall having been only 2-31, the water, which was good the previous year, became so impure that 60 per cent of the new locomotive power could not be used.

I have pointed out that we have had very dry seasons when there were scarcely any complaints and when there was no complaint of the alkali, simply because the water supply was looked after. Hut because it was neglected later, because the tanks were allowed to get our of order, through false economy in not keeping sufficient men to look after them, and because the wells were not kept clean, there was cause for these complaints. I have a good word to say for many of the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I think they do all they can, and I think, if their reports and suggestions were taken into consideration a little more at the head office, the people of the west would not have so many grievances.
As regards to what my hon. friend from St. Mary's division of Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said about the unpatriotic manner in which some of the people of the west had insisted in bringing about such a state of affairs, that several charters were granted last session by the Manitoba parliament to the Great Northern people, to build roads into this country, let me tell the hon. gentleman that, so far as we are concerned, I never heard of any such agitation. As a matter of fact the Northern Pacific, which is now practically a part of the Great Northern, was brought into the province of Manitoba years ago. We had them in there, and my hon. friend might have gone further and told ns how it was that they were driven out of the province. I do not know whether be would call that a patriotic action or not, but they were driven out of the province, and I am not aware that they wanted to come in since. The fact that some people applied for a charter does not warrant my hon. friend in saying that Jim Hill got it. It is well known that Sir. Hill has denied that he had anything to do directly or indirectly with the charter granted by the Manitoba legislature. But no doubt some persons thinking that there might be something in it, has applied for a charter, and we may hear something about it a little later on. As far as my part of the country is concerned, we have nothing to do with it. But if we want to get connection with an American road, I would like my hon. friend to tell me why we have not as good a right in the west to have connection with American roads as the older portions of Canada.
If you build your own railways, but not if you build them with our money.

I do not know that this particular company to which my hon. friend from St. Mary's was alluding has asked for any money. If my hon. friend knows of any money they have asked for he is better informed that I ; his political friends are connected with it.
I know what money you are trying to get now.	' '

I think we have a precedent for that sort of thing, and the less the hon. gentleman says about it the better. I could refer the hon. gentleman to that piece of railway which was built through Slaine by the same company which my hon. friend talks about.
And which led to a great Canadian jjort.

A Canadian road led to the same part, but this was the piece of line subsidized by Canadian money to be built on American soil-going in and out again, as my hon. friend has said. But was it patriotic for us to subsidize a railway to be built on American territory to compete with our own national road ? No one has ever pressed such a demand as that from this side of the House. The railway asked for is a line just reaching to the boundary. No one have ever asked this government to put their hands into the treasury and subsidize a road built on American territory. But that was done years ago by a Conservative government. We have the Grand Trunk Railway running into Portland. That was done in the good old days. My hon. friend might tell us something about that. Was that unpatriotic ? You have I do not know how many roads running across the boundary line in order that you may do business with the Americans. You have to do business with them. They are our neighbours. And if it is good for the people of the east to have a connection across the line with the Americans and do business backwards and forwards, it also would be a very good thing for us. The sooner the people of this country realize that we in the west have not a sucking bottle In our mouth the better it will be for them. We have a right to say something about our affairs without being lectured for lack of patriotism. One thing strikes me, and that is that out of the contingent of western members from the country west of the lakes there was not one to be found to defend this proposition, and a man had to be got from the east, who appears with a big brief, and who is not posted on western matters as he should be. True, he made a couple of trips and there was no lack of cars-of private cars anyhow
I shall come again.
I hope to see my hon. friend there. We will welcome him, but I am afraid if he takes the line of argument he did this evening in the House and accuse our people of being unpatriotic^
I never made any such accusation.

It was an implied accusation. It was an insinuation. I think the House will bear me out in saying that we were accused of trying to hamper a great Canadian industry and all that sort of

thing. I shall not take up any more time as other speakers will follow. The Canadian Pacific Railway have done a good deal for this country and I would like to see them prosper. We do not want to see then injured in any way, but when they can pay 6 per cent on their stock and have power to issue .$20,000,000 more, on condition that $9,000,000 should be spent in the west in motive power and in doubling their tracks. We would like to see-them carry out their agreement. That line has to be double tracked from Moosejaw to Port Arthur. Sidings and all that sort of thing will not relieve the congestion. If they have a double track from Moosejaw to Port Arthur with sufficient rolling stock, they can carry all the wheat out from that part of the country. Other portions of the territory will be served by the Canadian Northern. We have grievances, and it is not only good for the people but for the Canadian Pacific Railway that we should ventilate them. The Canadian Pacific Railway will find out that if they would adopt a more live policy in dealing with the west, it would be a benefit to themselves. Perhaps after the discussion this afternoon we may find them buying more locomotives and rolling stock. If they cannot buy them, they can manufacture them. The people of the west have the interests of the Dominion as much at heart as the people of the east, notwithstanding what my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has said this evening. I think you will find as much patriotism in the west as in any part of this Dominion. I need only go back to three years ago, when the empire needed volunteers. Who were the most ready to volunteer ? Who more ready than the men of the North-west ? And very good soldiers they proved themselves, and a very good showing they made.
Hear, hear.
speakername: The MINISTER OP MILITIA AND DEFENCE.

speechtext: The people of the west have insinuated that they are not loyal or that they desire to sever that portion of territory from the empire and annex it to the United States.

It is not very often that the members for Manitoba and the North-west have an opportunity of taking part in a discussion that comes so near to them as the one brought before the House this afternoon by the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott). For that reason I feel disposed to occupy a few moments of the time of the House in discussing the question. I do not altogether agree with the remarks of the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) when he said, as I understood him, that it was not in the best interest of the country that the matter should be brought to the attention of the House in the manner it has been. For my part, I believe it is in the best interest of the country in more ways 78
than one that this subject should be thoroughly ventilated. There is no denying the fact that the people of the North-west Territories and Manitoba are not satisfied with the treatment they have received for the past two years and are still receiving. I admit that there is some excuse on the part of the I'ailway company. We have had an increased acreage in cultivation, and, for two years, the crops have been exceptionally heavy. The transportation, not merely of these crops, but of the goods, the purchase of which naturally attend the more prosperous condition of the country, has made an enormous traffic for the railway. The passenger traffic also has been unusually great. Last summer, the railways had to carry in 25,000 people, harvest labourers, and then take them out again. Then owing to the prosperous condition of the people, many more than usual have been able to visit friends in the east and return. This also has made an abnormal condition of affairs. These things must be considered. For my part, I do not wish to minimize the difficulties or to find fault unnecessarily with the railway company. They have certainly done a great deal. In other seasons what they have been doing lately, would have been accepted as a fair effort. Still, as I have said, there is no denying the fact that they have not met the requirements of that country and that, if they are going to remain in the country and if the country is to make the progress we all feel it ought to make, either the company must voluntarily do more than it has done, or this government or whoever is responsible in the premises, must take steps to meet the emergency which now exists.
The hon. member for St. Mary's spoke of granaries. As to this, I cannot speak for the North-west Territories, but I know that, so far as certain portions of Manitoba are concerned, there is more granary capacity for the number of people and the number of acres under cultivation than in any other part of Canada or the United States. I say that without fear of contradiction. There are men in Manitoba whose granary capacity is from 1,000 to 18,000 bushels. I know that my hon. friend from St. Mary's when he made his statement, either was not conversant with these facts, or else he was speaking of the territory further west, where the people are not so well supplied in this respect. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) speaks of the people being patriotic. He tells us that the people of Canada have done a great deal for Manitoba and the North-west. Well, we in Manitoba and the North-west feel that we have done a great deal for Canada; and, if you take away that portion of the country, you leave Canada very small. Rut I do not think matters should be discussed in that spirit. There is no question of the patriotism of the people of the North-west, nor is there any question what you may expect of them in the future.



But, if you wish to keep them patriotic, it would be better to make provision that complaint cannot be made by the representatives of the people of that country such as have been made here to-night. And I may point out to my hon. friend from St. Mary's that if he supposes that the grain of Manitoba and the North-west Territories is to be brought through Canadian channels, Canada must meet the requirements of that country. I understand that some 2,000,000 bushels of wheat went to Minneapolis, to lie milled there and passed out through the United States. How are you going to stop these people from coming in and buying the wheat and taking it out of the country ? Or how are you going to stop railways coming in and building lines and competing for the trade of the country ? I notice the same condition of affairs in this Hfmse this year as when a somewhat similar question was under discussion last session. There are just two ministers present while this important matter is being discussed, one of them being the Minister of Militia, our fighting man. I would ask the members for Manitoba and the North-west to ask the government if they think they are showing the interest in our affairs that they should show and that the people of Manitoba and the North-west Territories have the right to expect them to show. And, while they are asking the government this question, I would also like them to ask the government what they have done since they came into power in 1896 to meet the conditions that have been rising in that country, particularly within the last two years, and what we have to look for in years to come. We will forget, for the time-being what they did to prevent the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway into that country; we will forget the criticism they levelled at that enterprise and at the country; we will try to forget, in the kindness of our hearts, the things they said about us in those days. But I would ask what they have done for that country now that they are responsible for the future of the Dominion ? I expect that some of the ministers will rise in their places and point out what they have done. We have been trying to find that out. but none of the men in the North-west Territories have been able to discern it up to the present time. So far as building other roads into the country is concerned. I remember that when I first spoke in this Chamber, about 1893, I pointed to the present premier (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) who was sitting in opposition then, and said : If the hon. gentleman who leads the opposition will recant and say he is sorry for the things that the people whom he represents have said about Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and will go so far as to say that they have not done what they should have done, and that he will show his repentance by agreeing to the building of another road into that country-because by the Mr. BOYD.
time it is built it will be needed-then they might be looking for some support from that country. The hon. gentleman shook his head across the Chamber, and I said : The hon. gentleman shakes his head, but until he does something like that, he should not look for the support from Manitoba and the North-west Territories that he seems to think he deserves. Now, Mr. Speaker, the Liberal press, particularly the ' Free Press,' poured out* its vials of wrath upon me, because I had had the audacity to make such a suggestion as that. Well, Sir, after having lived up in that country for fifteen years, I recognized what was going to happen, and what has happened; and no act of the government now in power can be pointed out as having had any effect in relieving the situation, which has been caused by the greatness of that country itself and not by anything we have to thank the present government for.

I was surprised at the line or argument adopted by the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) in dealing with this question this evening. He takes a position that really was not advanced, and he sums up his whole argument by saying that this question is brought on to-day as a notice of motion that large bonuses are going to be laid upon the Table very soon. Now, Mr. Speaker, I want particularly to associate myself with the protest that has been made this afternoon; and at the same time I want to distinctly disassociate myself from sharing any information or any understanding as regards the inference that the hon. member for St. Mary's has drawn about this question being a notice of motion that parties are coming down here for bonuses in a few days. The complaint that has been raised to-'day is almost exclusively in regard to the present blockade, not outgoing but incoming. A blockade of incoming freight is the great thing that is being complained of at the present time. A deputation has been sent from the Winnipeg Board of Trade to the head offices in Montreal, asking the railway authorities to take some steps to distribute the freight that is already in the country, and has been lying in the sheds for weeks, but which the merchants cannot get at. At this time it is not the outgoing grain blockade that is being complained of. I certainly think that the members from the North-west are not only within their right but performing their duty in bringing this matter before the attention of the government and of this House. Because who else can we look to for redress ? They have not yet been able to get any relief, matters have been getting worse and worse.
But I rise now more particularly to refer to something that has not yet been touched upon, but which has had a material influence in causing the present freight blockade from Winnipeg clean through to the

Pacific coast. At the end of last year the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, through its secret service, became aware that a new and large organization was growing up on the western division of its line, an organization composed almost entirely of freight handlers and freight clerks. The company made arrangements to work a coup to break up that organization, to split it up before it had extended to the east. By the end of January they were ready, and they sent out their men from Montreal and commenced operations in Vancouver. Directly they took these initial steps, every man went out on strike, and they are all on strike to-day. They are not out for wages, they are not out for hours, nor is there any dispute about conditions, but they are out as a declaration that they shall not be discharged for belonging to this organization. To-day, from Winnipeg to Vancouver, the old freight hands on the Canadian Pacific Railway are not] at work, and that fact is the cause, to a great extent, of the tremendous blockade, the crippling blockade, that now exists in regard to incoming freight. Freight trains have been piled up in the Winnipeg freight yard, in the yard at Calgary, in the yards in the mountains, in the yard at Vancouver, and the company themselves do not know what is there. It is their policy not to recognize any new organization of their employees. With my hon. friend from Macdonald (Mr. Boyd), I regret that the members of the government do not stay in the House and pay more attention to these matters. The Minister of Labour has not taken any part at all in this trouble up there yet, but it is one of the matters that, if his department is to be of any use at all, it should have been dealing with for the last two months-not to help the company or to help the men, but to help the people of western Canada that are being held up through this blockade. I have now given you, Mr. Speaker, the chief cause of this blockade, and I charge without any hesitation that it was brought on by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and is deliberately maintained by them for that purpose.

As an Ontario man I have listened with a good deal of interest to this debate, which has been participated in by members from the North-west. I listened especially with interest to the campaign literature which has been delivered by the hon. gentleman who moved the motion (Mr. Scott). I am free to admit that I sympathize with the hon. gentlemen from the North-west over the situation they have described to us. I know something personally of the conditions that have prevailed for the last six months, and while they are bad enough, I do not think I could go as far as the hon. member for East Assiniboia has done, and charge the Canadian Pacific Railway Company with being robbers. I think that is going a little too far. But there is no doubt that the con-78 J
ditions which have prevailed during the past year have been almost intolerable. But I want to point out that the conditions have been almost as intolerable in the east. We, in Ontario, have suffered fully as much, I am sure, as the men engaged in shipping in the west. Not only do we suffer the inconvenience caused by the delay in shipping stuff to the west, but by the delay in shipping stuff backwards and forwards from Ontario to the seaboard and from one Ontario point to another. Hon. gentlemen have given their personal experience, which is perhaps more telling than anything else. I may say that during the spring just passed the delay.has been so great, not only on the Canadian Pacific Railway but on other roads, as to cause such inconvenience that we hardly know how to get along in shipping. Of goods shipped from the neighbourhood of Hamilton and the centre of the province of Ontario, in large lots, fully half of those shipments this spring were eight days in travelling from one to two hundred miles. When you compare that condition of things with the shipping facilities that prevail in England, for instance, you will agree that they are abominable. Why should goods shipped from the neighbourhood of Hamilton and the centre of the province of Ontario be eight, ten or twelve days in travelling one or two hundred miles, as fully half of the shipments have been this spring ? It may be said, and I believe with a good deal of truth, that the amount of traffic is unusually heavy, and there is no question about that. But the roads ought to have prepared for the traffic. What would be thought of a merchant, a manufacturer, or a farmer whose business was increasing and who made no preparation for it ? What would a merchant, a manufacturer or a farmer do if in anticipation of a double production of goods he did not prepare to double the number of his hands and the means for conveying those goods to market ? Well, that is the position of the railway companies. They must have foreseen two or three years ago that the trade was rapidly increasing and they should have made provision then for meeting the condition of things which exists to-day. I have gone frequently to the managers of the roads complaining of this condition of affairs and they have told me that they did not doubt that what I said was true but that they had made every effort possible to buy locomotives and cars in every available place not only in Canada but in outside countries as well. They have told me that every workshop for the building of cars in Canada is taxed to its utmost capacity and that they are placing upon the roads all the locomotives and cars they can get. Doubtless that is true but my complaint is that they have not made greater preparation years before because this is a condition of affairs that might have been anticipated in a country like Canada. I was conversing with a gentleman from Glasgow

and he said that goods were carried between London and Glasgow in thirty-six hours, that he could order goods in London and be sure of receiving them in Glasgow within that time. We know that such a condition of affairs has never existed in this country, saying nothing about the last year or two when traffic had been unusually heavy. It was never known years before. It has always taken about six days for goods to go 100 or 200 miles in Ontario. I maintain that the railways of Canada are not managed on as good business principles as they might be. I can give one instance where an attempt has been made to carry goods quickly. The Michigan Central Railway will carry fruit from Winona to Petrolea and other places in the western peninsula of Ontario in sixteen hours. Some effort should be made by the railways to carry fruit at a quicker rate than that which now prevails. No doubt conditions that prevail in a new country where traffic is increasing rapidly are very different from those to be found in older countries. But there is a grievance existing all over the Dominion of Canada to-day in reference to railways. The railway companies say they are doing all they can possibly do to handle the traffic. It is a question whether it is not a matter of economy with them to provide just sufficient rolling stock so that the rolling stock may be employed the year round and so that the hands employed in the operation of these railways may be engaged the year round. That might be a matter that might very well be inquired into by the government. We have heard something about a railway commission to be appointed. It seems to me that the first matter that the railway commission should take up is the matter to which I have just referred. They should see whether the railway companies are providing all the means in their power to handle the traffic and whether they are making sufficient efforts to carry on the business of the country profitably. Hon. gentlemen from the North-west Territories complain of the loss and inconvenience in moving wheat out of the country. Wheat is an article that if it is not taken out to-day can be taken out to-morrow or next week, it suffers no great toss unless there is a fall in the market and it takes chances of a rise in the market. But it is different in regard to fruit. In Ontario, if you cannot get cars quickly, the fruit perishes. I am sure that last fall I lost several thousands of dollars owing to the delay in getting cars. Grapes stood on the platform for six days awaiting cars and they depreciated in value. The same thing occurs in the fall of the year in regard to apples. I believe that the apple shippers of Ontario last fall lost 40,000 barrels of apples w'hieh were frozen because it was impossible to get cars to ship these apples. We do not usually have so favourable a fall. It was the 10th of December before apples would Mr. SMITH (Vancouver).
freeze in box cars. I remember a season when apples were frozen solidly on the 16th of November. If we had had such a season as that last fall we would have lost one-third of the apple crop of Ontario for lack of cars at the proper time. I do not wish to say that the railway companies did not do all they could do on the spur of the moment. I believe they made every possible effort at that time to get cars but the effort was not made soon enough. Now, it seems to me that we have the right to insist that the government shall take vigorously hold of this matter. The railway companies owe the public a great deal. The Dominion of Canada, the provinces and the municipalities have donated in the neighbourhood of $250,000,000 to these railways and what have we got ? We have the Intercolonial Railway, a railway that for some years, at any rate, has lost the money of this country to the extent of a dollar for every man woman and child every year and which has lost $2,000,000 or $3,000,000 every year if we count interest on the money invested in the road. Then, surely the public have the right to inquire into the affairs of these railways and to see if they have the proper equipment to enable them to do all they possibly can do to further the interest of the Canadian people. It is the duty of the government to see that this matter is investigated. It is the duty of the government, either by way of a commission, or through the Railway Committee of the Privy Council, to investigate this matter and see if the railways are doing all they can and to bring such pressure to bear as will compel them to do more than they are doing if that is possible.

I think my hon. friends from the west will only have the present government to blame if it is thought not only by a number of members of this House but by the people generally throughout the country that the grievances which they have brought up to-night is to us the first, and perhaps to some extent, distinct news of the fact that the government intend to bring down to the House a proposition in regard to the building of a new railway in the North-west. There is no doubt, and I brought the matter to the notice of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) some time ago, that we should have had before this day, laid before us the proposition which at the present moment is being matured around

tlie lobbies of this House in respect to railway construction in the North-west Territories. There is no doubt about that and the fact, brought to the notice of the House by the hon. member for Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee) that throughout this discussion the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) has been absent from the House, or, throughout the major part of it and has taken no interest whatever in the grievances which my hon. friends have sought to ventilate, will only add strength to the supposition prevailing everywhere that this is merely the first attempt on the part of the government-I do not pretend to accuse my hon. friends of anything of the kind-to prepare public opinion for some kind of a proposition which we will not be ready to accept. Now, my hon. friends have confined themselves

Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) permit me to make a brief statement ? I think he must entirely have misapprehended the trend of my remarks. I endeavoured to take pains to state that the question I was discussing was a question entirely apart from the building of new lines and not only that but that it was a question which could not be met by the building of new lines. It was a condition prevailing which had to be dealt with immediately this year and which could not be solved by any proposition to build new railways because no new line could be extended to the country in time to give the relief that must be had this year.

My hon. friend (Mr. Scott) confined himself largely to dwelling on the sufferings which the people of the Northwest were enduring, because of the congestion of traffic. He made an onslaught on the Canadian Pacific Railway but he had not a word to say against the government which announced in the speech from the Throne its intention to bring forward some legislation to remedy that state of affairs, and which has kept us two months here without announcing their policy. What has my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) to say against the government for that kind of conduct ? Not a word. I fully appreciate the suffering which the people of the North-west are enduring, but does the hon. gentleman imagine that we in the east have not grievances because of the blockade of the traffic on railways. My hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Smith) has spoken of the grievances of the people in the province of Ontario, and I can tell the hon. gentleman from Assini-boia (Mr. Scott) that in the province of Quebec at the present time, we are labouring under the same grievances. Let the hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) ask the member for Terrebonne (Mr. Desjardins) if during the recent election there the great cry was not the impossibility of the people getting cars for the absolute necessities of commerce. In fact there was no cars to convey wood
to the suffering poor of Montreal. At the present moment in Montreal the builders cannot get cars to bring stone from outside the city, to enable them to carry on their operations.
Why is that ?
Why ? My hon. friend knows that the same state of things exist throughout the Dominion, and in the United States as well.

The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in order to relieve the condition of things in the west, has drawn off the cars from the old provinces during the autumn months, and as a consequence you suffer in the older provinces. But still, the difficulty exists in the west and it is all due to the lack of the rolling stock on the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Then we have a grievance against you, and we have often been told of that in the province of Quebec. When we go to the Canadian Pacific Railway officials and complain, they tell us :	We have been
obliged to draw upon our rolling stock here to supply the necessities of the North-west. But that is a condition which exists to-day on the whole of the American continent. Let me read a letter which was sent to the New York 'Post' by Mr. Stuyvesant Fish, president of the Illinois Central Railway, a man of high reputation as a railway man, and I read the letter because it throws a flood of light upon the question we are discussing here this afternoon. Mr. Fish writes :
Sir,_The gravity of the situation in which
the railroads of the United States stand in respect to their very general inability to carry the freights now offering must excuse this, perhaps, too long letter.
The Interstate Commerce Commission has for some time past been inquiring into an alleged increase in rates by certain railroads in the territory east of Chicago and north of the Ohio river. From the accounts published in the newspapers it would seem that much testimony has been elicited showing that the cost of every item which goes to make up the expense of rendering the service has advanced beyond measure, particularly fuel, motive power, rolling stock, materials, wages, and taxes, possibly in the order named.
The discussion might, and I think should, be put upon the higher plane of sound public policy rather than on that of mere cost. The public demand that common carriers shall furnish transportation when, where, and as called for, without previous notice. Facilities equal to the maximum and far above the average demands of the public must be provided at all times. For years past so doing has not been limited by the willingness or the ability of the railroad companies to defray the cost, but by their incapacity to get men and material for the work.
The rates of freight and of fare now prevailing are substantially the abnormally low ones which the railroads *yere forced to accept in the bad times from 1893 to 1897, when their facilities vastly exceeded the demand for trans-

portation. The return of general prosperity has in all parts of the country created demands for transportation not only exceeding all previous experience, but growing with inconceivable rapidity and persistency.
Had the rates been advanced and kept in line with the price of other commodities and services, the demand for transportation would have been concurrently checked. This was not done, and as a result we find the Pennsylvania Railroad Company, which has in recent years raised the largest amount of new capital, and the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad Company, which has perhaps raised the next largest amount, blockaded at Pittsburgh.
Our situation on the Illinois Central is one of congestion, if not bordering on blockade, although within four years our capital stock has been increased from $52,500,000 to $95,040,000, through the payment into the treasury of $42,540,000 of money, which is more than 80 per cent of the amount which had been subscribed in the preceding forty-eight years, from 1851 to 1899.
Other companies all over the country have made proportionate expenditures on betterments, and all find their traffic congested. It is safe to say that with a ' bumper ' crop of corn yet to move, the demand for transportation has this winter been further in advance of the supply than at any former time, and it looks as if things would get worse before they get better.
The custom among railways was, until recently, to contract in January, and even later, for a supply of rails for the then current calendar year. The great companies contracted in May, 1902, for their supply for 1903.
As to locomotives and cars the situation is worse. We still lack one lot of engines which should have been delivered last July, and others for later deliveries, and some thousands of car3. I was to-day offered twenty-five locomotives for delivery in January, 1904, and told that no other works in the country could furnish them at an earlier date. It took our greatest locomotive works, the Baldwins, seventy years to build 20,000 locomotives. I understand they now have 2,900 under contract* of which 1,000 are for delivery in 1904.
In structural iron, and in material of all kinds, like instances might be multiplied indefinitely.
The thing runs around in a circle, working back, in every case, to the failure of some one to deliver something. What except the growing excess of the demand for, over the supply of, transportation has brought this about.
Having regard to the best interests of the nation at large, have we not reached a point where the railroad companies now owe it as a duty to the public to advance their rates to the end that those who tender money may get the service and get it promptly ? If not, can any measure of general relief be afforded in any other way ?
Very respectfully,
January 7, 1903.
Will my hon. friend permit me to ask a couple of questions ?
I do not want to take up the time of the House, but if my hon. friend makes his questions short, i will try to answer them.

Does the hon. gentleman think, that any one of the roads referred to
in that letter occupies the same position as the Canadian Pacific Railway does in its relation to the people of Canada ; the Canadian Pacific Railway being under specific contract to the people of Canada, for value received to give an efficient service.

There is no doubt that"the Canadian Pacific Railway Company-from whom I may say I hold no brief of any kind-has contracted obligations towards the country; but there is such a thing as not being able to fulfil those obligations; and the point which my hon. friend has endeavoured to make, and which I want to make, is that we in the eastern provinces are suffering as well as the people in the west.

I am quite satisfied with that statement. The next question is. will my hon. friend support the suggestion I have made that some step or action be taken to enforce the terms of that contract on behalf of the people of Canada ?

The answer to the questiO'ii which my hon. friend puts to me would be very much the same as to one which I have given to his previous question. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company must be urged, and I would support the urging of that company, to give satisfaction in the west as well as in the east. Possibly I would urge that we in the east, who have done so much to build that railway in the west, should be the first to be accommodated; lint at the same time, I must say, whether it is because we who live in the east are more reasonable than our young friends from the west, or for some other reason, we realize that to a large extent it is impossible for that company, as much so as it is for the Illinois Central or the other large American companies, to satisfy the demand fully. That is' one point I want to make. Another point I want to make is this. We are perfectly ready, once we know what the government's proposition is, to do the very best we can to help our friends in the Northwest, although we must recognize that the conditions are greatly changed from those which existed at the time the Canadian Pacific Railway was built, largely at our expense ; and I for one, speaking off-hand, will give great consideration to the principle now laid down in the constitution of every state of the American union, that the time is past when the railways being built should be aided by the state. I think that is a matter for serious consideration; but what I say is that at the present moment the question of facilities for transportation is not to be considered purely and simply from a western standpoint, and I think that is a just and' legitimte view to lay before this House when we hear our hon. friends expounding with so much vigour the difficulties' that exist in the North-west, with which I thoroughly sympathize, and for the relief of which I and I am sure my friends on this side of

247S
the House are willing to do everything that is possible. But while that is the case, we must not forget that the transportation question does not end on the shores of Bake Superior, but extends from the west down through Canadian territory, through the St. Lawrence river, and ends practically on the other side of the ocean; and the time has come when we who have made such large and important sacrifices to build up the west -and pleased we have been to make them- should be given some consideration in regard to the problem of transportation. Speaking more particularly for the locality from which I come, I ask of what use would it be to us if all the grain grown in the west came down to Montreal when we have there and at every other port in the province of Quebec such limited facilities for handling the traffic ? What has been done for the port of Montreal ? I say these matters must be considered simultaneously; and whilst we are ready to do everything in our power to aid the west, our hon. friends themselves, if they are affected by the patriotic feelings which they have spoken of this evening, and as to the sincerity of which I have no doubt, must at tlie same time consider that we in the east have great wants that must be attended to at ouce. 1 spoke a moment ago of what had taken place in the 'elections of Terrebonne and Two Mountains, where the grievance referred to by my hon. friend was one of the prominent subjects of discussion. In the division of Montreal, where we had a minister of the Crown coming forward for reelection, the question perhaps most discussed was the question of placing the port of Montreal and the navigation of the River St. Lawrence in such a condition as to make our national system of transportation a perfect one from the west down to the ocean. On that occasion the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Hon. Mr. Prefontaine) felt that question was one of such deep interest to the people of that section of the country, that lie pledged himself on every public platform where he spoke, that the first duty of the government would he to place the port of Montreal on the footing of a national port, because he declared to the electors that a transfer would be made to his department of every part of the public works which concerned transportation. What I say is this, that we are ready, as far as we are able to do so, to help our friends in the west on this question of facility of transportation; but at the same time they must not fail to consider that the question of transportation, on which we have had no declaration of policy from this government since 1896, is one which must be considered from the extreme west to. the extreme east, and I for my part will not be ready to make any undue sacrifices to help our friends in the west unless they are ready on their part to take a broad, national view of this question; because anything we may do now in
the west alone would have the effect undoubtedly of diverting the traffic of the west into: American channels. I therefore wish not to be understood in any sense as hostile or as unwilling to consider the grievances which these gentlemen brought before us this evening; but at the same time 1 deem it my duty to call their attention in a friendly manner to the fact that the transportation question at the present moment is perhaps more unsolved in our part of the country than it is in theirs. Thi's question of transportation must he considered in its entirety, and while it is right for our hon. friends from the west to air their grievances in this House, it seems to me that we are equally entitled to call attention, in similar energetic language, to our side of the question. Let us have a complete national scheme of transportation, and whatever sacrifice it may entail on our part again- because that would be the second time tor our eastern provinces-I am quite ready that we should undergo these sacrifices, but it must be for a scheme considered from one end of the Dominion to the other.

I have no apology to offer, Mr. Speaker, for continuing the debate. It was not my intention to speak at any length, because I have not prepared notes, and was content to leave the matter very much in the hands of my hon. friend (Mr. Scott) who addressed the House this afternoon so moderately, ably and fully. I spolie on the question of the glraln blockades last session and I am pleased to find that the hon. member for AVest Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) 1ms pointed out the commercial aspect of the blockade. I would ask the House not to overlook this fact, that it is the business of the east which is being hindered in the West. It is the outgoing of your goods to our people which is being hindered and obstructed. You send your agents to the west by the thousand, they get their orders and the goods are sent out, but the people of the west find that the transit of these commodities is greatly impeded and obstructed. This therefore is not a sectional but a Canadian question, in which the people of the older provinces are just as much interested as the people of the West. On this question of the grain blockade, I could speak at some length. Having introduced grain legislation since 1896. in this House, I have kept my eye very closely on the conditions from time to time. During the months of January and February, I considered it my duty, as representing the people of Eastern Assiniboia, to visit all the branch lines and pay special attention to the condition of the grain trade on these lines. I went from town to town and from village to village and made my notes as to the effect of the legislation of last season, and I may state

very briefly that every siding was filled with cars loaded with grain. If there were any empties at all, they were in such a position that they could not be utilized. I found men shovelling- grain into cars from wagons in the winter snow when they could not reach them any other way. I remonstrated with these people and asked them why they went to such labour. But they said: We have as long as we choose to load these cars, because there is no engine to take them out; we can take a whole week, because when we have the car filled, it will stand perhaps two weeks before going out This was the condition of things on almost every siding all through these branch lines, at least in my constituency. But my observations were not confined to my own constituency, I took the trouble of travelling into Manitoba and found the same condition of things existing there.
We have found to-night members of the opposition endeavouring to find excuses for the railway company. If they do not support the Canadian Pacific Railway in the condition of things which exists to-day in the West, they! at least try to make excuses for the company. One excuse made by a leading official for Winnipeg in the city of Montreal, was that our legislation last year had greatly hindered the transport of grain by giving the farmers twenty-four hours to load a car. I wish to say that that statement is entirely unfounded because the ears, after they were loaded, stood two and three weeks and sometimes months before they were,moved, and furthermore the farmers who had paid demurrage because they had been two or three hours over the twenty-four in loading the car, had the pleasure of looking at the loaded car week after week before it went to market. I need not tell you that this delay is very serious. We have been told that we should submit to the inevitable, that we are a long way from the seaboard, and cannot expect to get our grain out in two or three months. Well, our people are reasonable, but when we have the grain of two harvests in our granaries, when we sell fatted animals from our ranches in August and cannot get them out of our way before the end of November, are we to be told that we should submit to the inevitable and that we ought not to vent our grievances in this House ? Is it not our duty, as representatives of a great grain growing community, to speak for the people ; and in doing so, we speak for the people of our Eastern provinces as well as our own. Our interests are mutual. If the west is prosperous, every wholesale merchant in Montreal, Toronto, Plamilton and elsewhere, will reap the' benefit, so that you cannot draw the line and say that this is a western question. We do not like to be told that we are unreasonable or not loyal. The old British flag has always been my pride. I delight in it still, and would be glad to see Mr. DOUGLAS.
all the produce of the west reaching the seaboard over Canadian routes, so that what has been said in that regard by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken has my hearty concurrence. We have been always ready to vote any money asked for the improvement of the St. Lawrence and the harbour of Montreal, and I trust that we will always be found ready to do the same again. Every dollar spent to improve our routes to the seaboard and our sea ports will benefit the west as well as the east. We do not want to be unreasonable fn our criticism even of the railway company. I believe that they are making vigorous efforts to meet the emergency. I believe them when they tell us that they will have 114 engines available before next season and that they are spending a large amount of money to meet present conditions, but what I do complain of is that they did not listen to the people who understood the development of the West years ago.
Five or six years ago they were told that they would not do the work of the country even with a double track-and I do not think they would be able to do it even if their track were doubled to-day. Further, they did not listen to their own officials in the North-west. They were very slow to receive instructions from those in their own employment who knew best what the conditions were. Now, they are up against a difficulty, and the people have to suffer, and they are told they must suffer patiently and loyally. The excuse has been made that it was the water supply-and the hon. member for St. Mary's, Montreal, has been eloquent about the water supply. The hon. gentleman forgets that, while the engines died on the track for want of steam power, the people all through the country there lived-even when it was so dry, as we are told, that there was no water for the engines. I am surprised that he overlooked that fact. The people there had water abundantly to meet their own needs and water their stock. Yet, a few, engines of the Canadian Pacific Railway could not find water enough to keep the breath of life in them. The fact is, the difficulty did not lie in the want of water, though we are told that sixty per cent of the engines could not be used for this reason. Then we are told that the water was bad. I have not much sympathy with that statement. The water certainly ought to have been much better during the last twp years than during the preceding eighteen years, for we had a great deal more rain. Every place was filled with water. And the more you dilute the alkali, the weaker it becomes. To say that there was a lack of water is scarcely an excuse for a company that has such facilities for securing money that it can go to Europe and, in a single season dispose of bonds that bring ,$17,000,1X10. Surely such a concern might have provided some

means of purifying and cleansing the water. Why, this very evening I received a letter from my own town of Moosomin, which is under contract with Messrs. Sutcliffe & Muir to build a merchant flour mill. And this enterprising firm-I think they are from the United States, though I have not the pleasure of their acquaintance-would not go into the business until they had solved the question of the water, and the effect of the water upon machinery. They took the trouble to send a sample of the water to analysts in Chicago, and I have here the analysis by these gentlemen. Messrs. Dickman, McKenzie & Potter. This contains the whole story of the water from Moosomin, one of the worst places in this respect along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I shall not trouble the House with this analysis, but I may say that the water contains sodium chloride, sodium sulphate, calcium sulphate, sodium carbonate, magnesium carbonate, silica and iron oxide and alumina in certain proportions. The impurities amount to 127-28 grains to the gallon. This enterprising firm of Sutcliffe & Muir has found a process by which all these impurities can be eliminated, and they write me to ask me that I use my influence to get some consideration from the Minister of Customs relative to the duty of 25 per cent on the machinery required for this purpose which comes from Chicago. Here is a private enterprise and before they introduce machinery into their mill they solve the problem of the water question. Why cannot the great Canadian Pacific Railway spend a little of their money in eliminating the corroding element of the water that probably caused damage last winter ? X am not prepared to say that they had very great difficulty in getting a water supply, 1 know the water in the town of Moosomin is very bad and I am very glad that enterprising town, which has introduced the telephone and electric light, is seeking to secure perfectly pure water for the use of the people. This is an idea that might very readily be taken up by the railway company and that might solve the question of the running of their railways during the winter. My own idea is that the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) struck the keynote when he said :	They had not shelter for their
engines, and they had not enough engines to allow each a day at proper intervals to be cleaned up and properly prepared to go to work again. In consequence, many of the engines came to grief.
Reference was made to the Bill respecting the grain trade that passed the House last year. It was said that it was causing trouble, and the hon. member for St. Mary's asked us whether or not a meeting was held In Brandon to find fault with the measure. A meeting was held in Brandon, not to find fault, but to make some additions to the law to make it more effective. It is true that exception was taken to a single phrase.
It was suggested that the phrase 'without undue delay,' relating to the furnishing of cars, should be eliminated. And no objection would be made if these words were removed. But it is a wrong impression to leave on the minds of hon. members that the farmers are opposed to the Bill of last year. 1 am prepared to say from personal knowledge, having travelled over the branch lines, as I have said before, that the farmers are favourable to that law. The statement of those on these lines was to the effect that one who had shipped his own grain over the loading platform, had gained at the least calculation, nine cents a bushel. What does that mean ? It means, on the crop of this year a gain of some $4,500,000. So, we think we have a right to speak and to expect to be heard. We think we have a right to ask the House to consider the interest of these people who have lost immensely through the condition of things that have existed during all these years. The hon. gentleman stated that the gain by the farmers who shipped directly to the lakes, might be seventeen cents. I am prepared to support the hon. member in that, and I know cases where such a result was realized. Personally, we have shipped grain the same way, and got the benefit. I have heard both Liberal and Conservative farmers speak in unqualified terms of the advantage of the Bill. What they want is more facility for loading directly, what they want is to be allowed to take the car that is allotted to them to the elevator, and have it reckoned to their account and not to the elevator's account. The agents of the railway company have insisted all along the line if a farmer ordered a car to the elevator they should charge the car to the elevator and not to the farmer. I believe that an unlawful advantage has been taken of the legislation in that way. There are some conditions that might be improved that would make it much more efficient than it is today, but it has been an untold benefit to those who have made use of it.
If I had time to-night I could give you many facts similar to these given by my hon. friend from West Assiniboia. I could put my hand in my desk and give you testimony of grain growers' associations, boards of trade, agricultural societies and various associations interested in that trade, referring to the blockade, not only from a grain standpoint but also from a commercial standpoint. I hope that the facts which have been brought before the House will be carefully considered, and that some means will be adopted to relieve the west; and by relieving the west and assisting the business of the west, the eastern provinces will receive a like benefit, and perhaps a greater benefit. I quite concur in the arguments made, and the cases which have been brought before the House by my hon. friend from West Assiniboia. But my mind is not at all changed. I think we should in-

sist that when railway companies come for charters as they do, stretching their hands over the entire country, endeavouring to blanket the country with railway charters, this House should be exceedingly careful in granting any further charters until these companies show their ability to operate and complete the construction of the roads that they now possess. I dare say to-morrow there will be a warm discussion in the Railway Committee between the two parties now in the field seeking to construct roads into that country. It would be a wise thing if we restrained these railway companies in securing further charters until they show that the roads they now possess and operate are fully equipped. What advantage is it for us to open up a great country, in Mackenzie Basin for example, when there are no people there ? We are told that people will go there. But what about people that are going into the country now, if their wants are not met? What about all the immigrants that have gone in this season if they cannot get a thousand feet of lumber to put a floor under their feet and to cover their houses ? What about these people years hence when they have stuff to bring out and there is no railway to bring it out ? There are people who have been waiting for twenty years to get railways. I know the difficulties that exist in my own constituency. There is a proposition to extend a road this season, and we should be glad to see the road built. Here is a road to be extended from Moose Mountain to Regina. Well, it goes through a good country, there has been a large immigration into that district from the United States. There are people north of Qu'Ap-pelle in the same riding who have been raising 0,000, 8,000 or 10,000 bushels of grain, and have been forced through circumstances to haul it twenty, or thirty miles, and some of them forty miles, and that for eighteen or twenty years. Now, if our railway companies would think less of the other fellow and more of the needs of the country, it would be a great deal better for the west.
Will the hon. gentleman say who the other fellow' is ?

The other railway company that is seeking to get hold of the business. It is like a game of chess. When the other fellow' is about to move, then his opponent will move in advance, so you have competition to gain territory, not to build railroads, not so much to meet the immediate wants of the people, as to blanket the country with railway charters. I think a great responsibility is resting upon this House at this time. We want all the railways that W'e can get, and I would be glad to see the country covered to-day with rail-w'ays wherever there is a settlement. AVe do not wish to see a competition of the kind that is indicted, what we want is to Mr. DOUGLAS.
satisfy the people that are now in the country. My immigration policy has always been to give the people that are in the country the conditions of success, and they become the best immigration agents. At present, through the good crops of the last two or three years, our North-west country is in the eye of Europe, in the eye of the world. Success will secure settlers. But if the settlement of these people is hedged about with great difficulties, if these people are not carefully housed in the coming winter, if they have not railway facilities to take out the little grain that they may raise within a year or two, then they are in straits, they are in difficulties; and you will have them leaving the country as they have done before. going away in bitterness of spirit, writing in the newspapers against the country, believing themselves betrayed and victimized, and decrying the North-west Territories. It is for us clearly to consider the whole situation, and by some immediate steps seek to meet it. But we disappoint these people, we discourage these people. I hope that the government will seriously consider the facts that we have placed before them. AVhile we are in earnest inspeaking on behalf of our constituents, it is not for political purposes. I deny that in toto. AVe are speaking in the interest of the people who have cast in their lot with us, and who are seeking to make homes for themselves and their families. It is for us to keep our eyes open and our hands active in order to meet successfully every emergency that may arise.

I understood that the seconder of the motion, having withdrawn his action, the motion to adjourn the debate was in order. I did not think the motion could be disposed of while the hon. gentleman was on his feet speaking. The hon. gentleman was standing all the time, otherwise I would certainly have availed myself of the right to speak.
