speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Compton (Air. Pope) has the floor.

Air. Speaker.
I have listened with keen attention to the debate that has taken place in connection with this very important subject which has been brought to the notice of the House by the hon. member for AArest Assiniboia (Air. Scott). I fully realize, as I visit the great west every year, the importance of

its development and I also realize that while it is an important portion of Canada it is only a portion of Canada. It is not tlie whole of Canada and cannot be treated separately in many particulars and certainly not in regard to the transportation problem from the! rest of Canada. We must first consider the most important point of responsibility. If we have not sufficient facilities for transportation in the great west of Canada for the settlement that is going into that portion of the country and if people are 100 and 200 miles from railways somebody is responsible for it. If the condition of rates and if the accommodation for the traffic of that country are not what thfey ought to he somebody is responsible. Parliament is divided into two parts. One portion ot it is the opposition which has no power to operate but which has only power to crit1-cise. That portion of parliament which has power to put measures in force and to operate in the direction of benefiting the people of Canada is the government of Canada. If these hon. gentlemen from the west have any right to appeal to parliament they have the right to bring pressure to bear upon the government which they stand so faithfully behind, which they support on each and all occasions which they will blindly vote for through thick and thin and which they will not vote against on this or any other question during this entire session. If there is a responsibility, and I claim there is a responsibility, it rests upon the other side of the House, it rests with the government of the day, because they have been marking time ever since they have occupied the honourable positions which they now fill rather than studying the requirements of the country and providing for them. They are up against it to-day. This is not the first time that I have spoken upon this subject. This is not the first time that I have given warning to this government that they would find themselves in a difficulty in that country. I spoke on the subject last year and the year before and the year before that and I notified the government then that they were not realizing what was about to happen in the west. They were not realizing the necessities that were going to spring upon them in that region of Canada and to-day they have hon. members from that country who support them, because they have the four territories, as represented'in this House behind them, standing up one after the other and condemning the government for neglecting to realize the responsibility which rests upon them in connection with this matter. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Scott) smiles. Does he propose that parliament. shall operate as a parliament without the government ? What does he mean when he asks the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) if he would join him ? Join him in what ? As a member of this House ? Join him in going outside of this House, or in bringing force to bear ns a
member of this House ? He has no power and no right, except a personal right, to ask the hon. member for Jacques Cartier as a member of this House to join him in bringing pressure to bear upon the government. There is no sense or reason in any other position than that and when the hon. gentleman asked the hon. member if he would join him he simply aslcad if the opposition in this House would join him in forcing the government to take such action as he thinks is essential to the welfare of the country. Otherwise his request is meaningless. But, there is one thing that has become chronic with these hon. gentlemen. For twenty long years, or at least during a considerable portion of those twenty years, the then opposition, the then Liberal party, spent their time denouncing the Canadian Pacific Railway, denouncing the Conservative party for supporting any syndicate^ in the construction of that road, denouncing the country through which that road ran, and denouncing the freight rates which had to be high in the beginning because there was very little to take out of the country. This spirit of criticism became chronic with these hon. gentlemen. It has settled down upon them like a fog, it rests upon them, they see through that fog the Canadian Pacific Railway and they say that the Canadian Pacific Railway is the curse and the bane of this country. That is the miserable misfortune of the party that has been denouncing this great project for years. What do we find, Sir ? We find that a certain party, fortunately or unfortunately, found themselves intrusted with power, they found themselves placed in a position to govern half of the continent of America and they found themselves under the necessity of grappling with the great problem of transportation after twenty years of denunciation of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have travelled through the territories and the only extension which has been encouraged or constructed under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite of railway is a short line running from Lethbridge to the Crow's Nest Pass. Not another link in the railway system of the west has this government constructed, not a spike has been driven in these territories.

I would remind the hon. member (Mr. Pope) that for five years before 1S9G. except the Soo line between North Portal and Pasqua junction near Moose Jaw, not a single line of railway was built in the North-west Territories, while at this day, there are no less than five railways being extended from the Manitoba boundary into the territories.
Is there a railway from Regina to Prince Albert ?
Yes.
Under whose administration was that road built ?
That road was built about twelve years ago.
By the Conservative party V Who built the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway ? You will own that before you get done. Under whose administration was the road built from Calgary to Edmonton ?
It was built with the laud of the North-west Territories.

Yes, with the lands of the North-west Territories and why not ? Do they want my land in the eastern townships to build roads in their own section of country '( It was the system of the whole continent of America. Who first spoke of land grants in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway ? Did you ever hear of the administration of the late Alex. Mackenzie in this country ? Did you ever hear of his advertising to the whole world for a syndicate that for so many acres of land and so many million dollars would undertake to construct that road ? He established the principle of land grants and hon. gentlemen sitting over there, if they are not willing to father their past history, should repudiate it, but if they are willing to father it they should put that into their pipes and make the best construction of it they can.
One gentleman opposite tried to make us believe that because the Canadian Pacific railway runs through a corner of the state of Maine, it was thq same thing as if we were taking the wheat of the North-west to ship it through a United States port. No such comparison can he made. Unfortunately for Canada the international boundary line was defined by incompetents and consequently a part of the state of Maine juts into what should be Canada, and in order to reach the port of St. John by the shortest route the Canadian Pacific railway has to pass through a comparatively short piece of American territory. But that is for the benefit of the people of the North-west because they get the advantage of a shorter haul for their wheat, and that wheat the Canadian Pacific railway ships across the Atlantic from a Canadian port. The hon. gentleman who used that argument has the reputation of having an inventive turn of mind, and I am sorry that he was so driven to the wall that he could not invent a better argument than that against our national railway. I agree that all Canada has been slow to realize the great possibilities of the west.
I believe that the Canadian Pacific railway itself has been slow to realize the possibilities of that great country. But none have been so slow as the government who are sending immigrants into that country to-day 200 miles ahead of a railway, when if they had foresight and a proper sense of their responsibilities, the Canadian Northern would long ago have received the assistance it is going to-receive and would a year ago

have been built into the Saskatchewan valley. I have no doubt that that line will not get a land subsidy and they should not get a money subsidy, but I believe it will receive encouragement so that it can finance its undertaking. If the government of the day had one half the confidence in the west that it should have, the Canadian Northern would now be completed to Edmonton. Look at the confidence of the old Tory party in the North-west; look at how they insured the building of railroads when there was not a white man or a bushel of wheat in all that territory, and compare the confidence of the Conservative government with the dilatoriness of the present government whicli hesitates to encourage railroads now that there are 100,000,000 bushels of wheat grown for export there, and hundreds of thousands of active and enterprising settlers tilling the soil. What do you think of these four gentlemen on the other side who have spent hours in fault finding to-day, but who, on every occasion, will continue to vote for the government like so many blind mice. If they want to have their point carried with the government, let them show to the gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches that they meant what they say. Let me show gentlemen that independence of action is as necessary in this House as independence of thought, they are only fooling the people of the west until they show that if the government does not carry out their wishes they will take means to urge them to action. It is all very well for the rev. gentleman from East Assiniboia (Mr. Douglas) to preach a beautiful sermon here. It was couched in very mild language. Why, if the whole fourteen ministers had been here instead of only one, not a single one of them could have the least fault to find with the kindly remarks of the hon. gentleman. He told us lie waited twenty years for a railroad. How long does he think the Barr settlers will have to wait if the government does not do any more to encourage railroads in the North-west than they have done during the past six or seven years. Who has been at the back of the opposition to the Mann & Mackenzie road ? Why is this that we have received maps from the Grand Trunk Railway Company showing their line running up and down Mann & Mackenzie's right of way; recognizing the Canadian Pacific railway but ignoring the Mann & Mackenzie road. I say Sir, that there has been an effort on the part of some one to take Mann & Mackenzie by the throat, but the circumstances which have arisen have forced the government to action. It was not their forethought or their confidence in the west that prompted the government to activity. It is through a chain of circumstances which has arisen which now forces the government to act, and if an effort had not been made to stifle Mann & Mackenzie in their infancy we should have three transcontinental roads now instead of two. With all its faults we have to thank the Manitoba government that Mann & Mackenzie were able to stand the financial attack on them, and with their line pointed towards the Saskatchewan valley, defy some of the senators and some of the members of this government and some of the financial institutions of this country. Some lion, gentlemen on the other side have stated in this parliament to-day, that you cannot get transportation into that country or out of it and amongst other things they said that the farmers have to pay ten per cent interest. All that is a bad advertisement for the west, and these supporters of the government might have omitted that from their remarks. They blame the Canadian Pacific railway but they should have followed the true rule of British parliamentary government and held the occupants of the treasury benches responsible for the existing condition of affairs. These gentlemen in. trying to serve two masters; in trying to advocate the interests of their constituents and at the same time defend the government which has not these interests at heart, have made a pitiable exhibition in this House. They tell us that they hold the Canadian Pacific railway responsible. Nonsense. The Canadian Pacific railway is not the government of Canada and it is the government of Canada that is alone responsible. Sir, I hold the government of Canada responsible; first for the want of railway communication into that country; and second, because there is not to-day a second transcontinental line traversing this territory and affording that relief which hon. gentlemen opposite claim is necessary. I say that if the government had done two years ago what they have to do to-day, that line would have been in operation, and you would have had a double track from the Great Lakes into the interior of that country. With regard to extra transportation or accommodation for that country, the government of Canada is responsible and no one else, and the hon. gentlemen who sit back there will in a few days, when the motion is made, be found supporting the policy of the government which has made that extra accommodation impossible; for we will take care that these hon. gentlemen have an opportunity of showing their independence of action as well as their independence of voice.

Mr. Speaker, I am not inclined to quarrel with my hon. friend who has just taken his seat when he says that perhaps neither the government nor the members of the House fully realized in the past the responsibility which devolved upon them, in view of the great development the North-west country was making, or we might previous to this have taken action to provide greater facilities	for the movement of the
grain and other products of the country in this era of prosperity. My hon. friend must remember, however, that for several years we had a period almost of stagnation, although many of us who had an opportunity of travelling through the-west did feel that in a short time, if our expectations were realized, there would be a great development in the settlement of the country, and a great deal of grain and other produce to be removed. I must say, however, that I think my hon. friend was a little severe in saying that during its term of office this government has not to some extent, and to a very considerable extent, taken steps to relieve the situation. I remember, when we were giving assistance to what was known as the Ontario and Rainy River Railway that one of the leaders of the hon. gentleman's party said that we were giving assistance to a road that was being built through a country that was barren and useless.
I am glad to know he was mistaken. The principal object of those who were supporting the road was to secure the construction of the most important link in the outlet from the west to Lake Superior. It was fortunate that that road was built, because it has been a great relief to the west. It is not my intention to speak on this question at any length; but I think the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) deserves the thanks of his constituents and of the country for bringing this matter to the attention of parliament, which he has done in a practical and argumentative speech. If he was severe in his criticisms of the railways, especially of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I think we can afford to be charitable to him for that when we. realize the difficulties which the people he represents have laboured under during the past season. The government, realizing the condition of affairs in the west, have from time to time made representations to the different railway companies, as to the great urgency of supplying more rolling stock and greater facilities for moving the grain and other products of the country. This is one of the most important questions that can come before this House. It is one affecting our whole national life, because I have always felt that, rates being about equal, it is very much to the interest of the farmers and other producers of this country that their products should be carried to the markets of the world by an all-Canadian route. In that way they will retain their identity, and every farmer and business man knows that Canadian products in the past have suffered from the fact that they have had to go through foreign countries, and in many cases have been replaced by the products of other countries, and have been made to appear in foreign markets ns inferior to what they are. The products of our farms are superior to those of almost every other country in the world, so that for the reasons I have stated, it is very important that we

should do everything we can to establish an all-Canadian route. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) reminded us that we must not forget the east. When I recall to him the fact that something over $0,000,000 has been spent on the St. Lawrence river channel and on the harbour of Montreal, it does not look as if the government had been forgetting the importance of establishing a national port in the harbour of Montreal.
speakername: The MINISTER OE PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. .Tames Sutherland).

speechtext: Not $6,000,000 in the harbour of Montreal.
The expenditure in the harbour of Montreal and the ship channel up to the present time has been over $6,000,000.
The money spent in the port of Montreal has been simply loaned money.
We are not going to quarrel about where the money came from. It was furnished by this parliament on the credit of the country. The money has been spent.
Will my hon. friend permit me to say that that is loaned money and we are paying interest on it.
The interest is by the traffic of the whole country, not alone by the traffic of the city of Montreal.
I wish to correct the statement made that the country has spent $6,000,000 on the harbour of Montreal. We in Montreal are paying interest on that money. [DOT]
The consumers of Canada who have been buying the goods that have passed through the port of Montreal have paid the interest on the money.
The government has not paid a cent of it.
The people of Canada who consume the goods passing through Montreal pay the interest on the Montreal harbour works.
That is very far fetched.
It is not far fetched; it is a well-known fact. That is no reason, however, why we should not deal handsomely with Montreal, as the great port of Canada.
Montreal is the only port where such a policy is carried out. On all other ports we are spending money and charging the country with the interest.

The money has been spent on those works as part of the national highway, and the credit of the country has been given to improve the port of Montreal. It is the Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
policy of the government, which I hope will be endorsed by parliament, to make these improvements not only at Montreal, but at other ocean ports. This is a great and important question, and it is desirable that we should look at it in the most careful and businesslike way. I think that my hon. friend from West Assiniboia (Mr. Scott) is to be congratulated for having brought this matter to the attention of the House, and 1 was rather sorry to hear some hon. gentlemen intimate that he had some motive other than that which he expressed in the remarks he made. There was not one sentence that would indicate that he had any other object except that of bringing to the attention of the House the conditions existing in the west, in order that any remedy which could possibly be applied should be afforded. I am perhaps inclined to differ with my hon. friend to some extent. It mav be possible that the Canadian Pacific Raif-way have.not done all they should have done. But many an interview has been had with the representatives of that company, and representations have been made by them, which I think ought to be accepted as satisfactory, that they were doing everything money could do to meet existing conditions. I hope that such is the case, and that the railway company as well as the government will be impressed with the urgent necessity of doing everything possible to advance the prosperity and progress which we all desire to see existing in this country. As a member of the government.
I think that I am expressing the views of my colleagues when I say that we will do everything possible in our power to relieve the situation.

I only intend to take a few moments of the time of the House. And in doing so, I wish to pay a tribute to the hon. gentleman who introduced this question. I do not think he was influenced by any other motives than those to which he gave expression. The fact that a certain important Bill is to be considered by a committee of the House and the fact that a certain document is being circulated among the members, may be considered as rather strange, coming together at this time, but I have no wish to attribute any motive to the hon. gentleman beyond those he has stated. I think he was quite right in bringing the matter before the House, but I regret that certain statements made here to-night should have been given expression to, and I am confident that when some hon. gentlemen read over their speeches in to-morrow's 'Hansard,' they will be very likely to cut out some of the statements they made, because to my mind, as a practical man, they were most erroneous and unfounded. I fail to understand why any hon. gentleman should, particularly in this House, make rash assertions affecting so large an enterprise as the Canadian Pacific Railway. We have been told, for in-

stance, that that line is in a deplorable con-! dition, that its management is very bad, and in fact it was really a dangerous line for any gentleman to travel on. That certainly cannot be the condition of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I have been in the employ of the Canadian Pacific Railway in my time, and I want to say, on behalf of the management-and I am in a position to express an opinion because I have had experience on several other lines in the United States and Canada-that as regards the congestion of traffic, the Canadian Pacific Railway have been trying, not for two years only, but for p large number of years, to secure sufficient engines and cars. When I was a member of a special committee in this House, appointed to look into the question of railway equipment, I found that the Canadian Pacific Railway and Grand Trunk Railway were both doing everything in their power to increase their rolling stock and meet the demands of traffic. As a matter of fact, it is utterly impossible for the railway companies of Canada and the United States to obtain the number of cars and engines they require. What are the conditions in the Northwest ? If I were to confine my remarks strictly to certain portions of Ontario, I would say that the rolling stock of any railway operated in those particular districts would last much longer and not require so many repairs as in Manitoba. Why? Because the conditions are different. In Manitoba they have, in the first place, the alkaline water to contend with, and then, during a large portion of the year they have to suffer from- severe frost. These are two things that railways have not to contend with in the section of the country from which I come. Then the Canadian Pacific Railway tried their utmost during last summer to secure a large number of machinists to go to Winnipeg for the purpose of repairing their engines. I am not rising as an advocate for the Canadian Pacific Railway, but simply to state the common sense practical views of a railway man on the question, given without fear or favour; and I do know, as a matter of fact, that the Canadian Pacific Railway were not able to secure machinists to repair their engines in Manitoba and in the North-west Territories. I may be asked why they did not import skilled labour from the United States. Well, the same difficulty exists in the United States. The railway companies there could not obtain machinists. These are actual facts. In a new country of the enormous size of the North-west and with its great traffic, the people will naturally have these grievances, and it is very unreasonable to expect the Canadian Pacific Railway to remove them entirely. One hon. gentleman stated here that the Canadian Pacific Railway inaugurated a strike in Winnipeg. Another hon. gentleman said that the company were so keen to declare dividends that they charged high rates, and so on. But if you will apply a little common sense to the question, whether you be a practical railway man or not, you will see that if the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway were so eager to secure dividends, the last thing they would dream of would be to foment a strike. Who ever heard of a strike on a railway being the means of creating a dividend ?
Is it not a well known fact that every strike on a railway is a source of great loss, not only to the company, but in many instances, to those engaged in the strike ; and when an hon. gentleman says that the Canadian Pacific Railway was actually responsible for this strike, he is making a statement so absurd that it is its own refutation. What else have we to consider 1 Is it not a fact that there is a large number of stockholders in this company, who are not all rich people, and who have their money invested in the shares of the company. Should we not be very careful then about making speeches in the House of a character that might possibly lead timid shareholders to dispose of their stocks and thus create a slump m the market. Hon. members should consider some of these things. If we have some persona] grievance against the Canadian Pacific Railway, let us state our grievance to the company, and if the company will not remedy it, then let us prefer specific charges and ask the government to investigate. And if the Canadian Pacific Railway is guilty, legislation should be prepared to prevent them creating grievances of that character The statement is made that the Canadian Pacific Railway allows cars to remain on the sidings for weeks and months.
I would like you to compare this statement with the one I am about to make. A year or two ago legislation was asked for and passed by this House allowing them to have cars on the sidings for not more than twenty-four hours. I want to ask my hon. friend who stated that cars are allowed to remain on the sidings so long, what would be the necessity

It is evident my hon. friend (Mr. Ingram) entirely misunderstands the question he is attempting to discuss. We did come down to the House and ask that the people should have the privilege of demanding from the company cars for direct loading, and last year, or the year before, the farmers of Manitoba and the Northwest were given that privilege. A statement was made here to-night in. answer to the excuse put forward on behalf ot the company that this direct loading privilege was responsible for the congestion of traffic. We pointed out, and pointed out truly that this had nothing to do with it, as was proved* by the fact that every siding was crowded for weeks and months last fall with loaded wheat cars.

And I have no doubt they will be crowded for years to come, for the

very reasons I have stated here to-niglit. To hear these hon. gentlemen speak, one would imagine that the company was not doing its duty in not having removed these grievances. Surely
If they would remove the loaded cars it would be all right.

But our hon. friends from the west forget the fact that, in the older parts of the Dominion we have the same difficulty to-day. Take the lines of railway that run through my own city, old established and well equipped lines that haul more cars in one train, probably than are hauled in two or three trains in the Northwest. Yet we have congested trade and are obliged to put up with it. We are exercising a little patience, I may say to these hon. gentlemen. After investigating whether the difficulty can be removed, and satisfying ourselves that it cannot, learning that the company are doing their best to meet the requirements of the service we exercise patience. Now, I say again that the statements made to-night are not correct; I have no hesitation in saying so. When they charge the Canadian Pacific Railway with being poorly and improperly managed, they are stating what is not the fact.
That is a matter of opinion.

So it might be. But my hon. friend (Mr Scott) must remember that we have this year an unprecedented rush of freight and passenger traffic in the Northwest. It is said that if a merchant expects trade to increase he will prepare for it. That is exactly what the railway companies are trying to do. But they are not able to secure the rolling stock and engine power, and naturally these grievances follow. If these hon. gentlemen can tell me that there is a car or engine factory, in this country that will supply the Canadian Pacific Railway with fifty or a hundred engines or with ten thousand cars, and the Canadian Pacific Railway has refused to *avail themselves of this opportunity to increase their equipment I will withdraw the statement.

The excuse is made that there is a lack of water. I can tell the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) that there are supplies of water that have been there for years and-I made this statement before- notwithstanding that the officers' of the company, years ago, recommended that these supplies of good water be utilized, it is only within the last month or so that the com. pany is making provisions for utilizing this water. The hon. gentleman from St. Mary's stated, as though he had the fact direct from the headquarters of the company, that 00 per cent of the power of the engines was useless last year because of the lack of good water.

The water and the weather combined-two very important elements in railroading-to put the engines out of repair. The severe weather during the winter months is a greater difficulty with regard to engines than any other they have to contend against, particularly when there is a lack of workmen to put the engines in repair. The company have done everything they could and, having done so they are not to blame. I have been told by a man from the west that a train starting with one engine, may require four engines before it can be moved. The alkali naturally affecting them so as to prevent them from steaming. We in easterm Canada have not this particular difficulty to contend with. We can do more work with one engine, probably, than can be done In the west with three. This greatly complicates the problem of running the road when there is a great rush of traffic. It is well for hon. gentlemen not to make too rash statements. They should bear in mind that the company have a great deal on its shoulders at the present time. I have no desire to run down the Canadian Pacific Railway, and no desire to praise it.
Oh, oh.

Some hon. gentlemen laugh. I would as soon praise the Grand Trunk or any other company that is making praise-worthy efforts to give the public a good service. I think that the Canadiau Pacific Railway notwithstanding what has been said deserves some little credit for what they have done. As eastern men we are willing to do what is right by our friends in the west. But they should not be unreasonable. They are progressing very fast and their requirements are growing with great rapidity. They must not be too impatient-
I trust they will excuse me for lecturing. If they will have a little patience they will get along very well.

At the risk of being considered somewhat tedious,
I desire to say a few words on this subject-
I am under the impression that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproulel has spoken.
I move that the House adjourn.
The hon. gentleniau. having spoken, has no right to make that motion himself.

I move that this House do now adojurn.

some of the suggestions that have been offered even if carried into effect, would not accomplish what the western members desire. The hon. member for Saskatchewan (Hr. Davis) said that the double tracking of the Canadian Pacific Railway would meet the difficulty. But a moment's consideration would show that this could not possibly be the case. The contention is that there is a blockade on the road' and that it is very inconvenient. No doubt it is. The difficulty is that there is much more freight and passenger traffic to be handled in a short time than there ever was before. But I might remind these hon. gentlemen that they are not alone in the experience of delay on the part of railways in handling freight. I am told by a business man in this section of the country that he had a car load of freight across the river from Windsor, twenty-three days -ago, the contents of which were consigned to him, and it has not been delivered yet. I think that is a fair parallel with what some of the hon. members have experienced in the west. The number of passengers that are going into that country at the present time, over 20,000 this spring, and the amount of settlers' effects to be hauled in, and the grain that has to be hauled out of that country, have certainly overtaxed the capacity of the railway. But that is an exceptional thing, and I think hon. members from the west ought to be as patient as possible. No doubt they are patient, to a certain extent, and we sympathize with them in the difficulties they have to contend with, and are as anxious as they to find a remedy. But that is not the only portion of the country that is suffering. What is the trouble in that country ? The increasing quantity of grain from year to year is such that no railway could handle it. Now, one hon. member said that double tracking the road would do it. Let me give him a calculation. Last year it was said there would be a hundred million bushels of grain to be disposed of. How many roads would be required to take that grain out of the country in the short time that the farmers desire it should be handled ? One road would not do it, two roads would not do it, three roads would not do it.
A hundred million bushels is a small amount of business for a good railroad.

I am told by one of the stockholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway that their large cars carry about 666 bushels, so that it would require 7,507 trains of twenty cars in each to handle that grain. At the rate of three trains a day, it would take 522 days. Now, if you had three roads hauling that grain, say each hauling twenty cars and three trains a day, it would take eighty-three days, or nearly three months, to handle that grain in the time that the farmers think it ought to be handled, between the time of threshing and the time that navigation closes.
I stated that the farmers did not ask that it should all be handled inside of three months, but they did complain when less than 25 per cent was handled in a season.

Well, the contention is that there is a blockade, and that the grain cannot be handled. I am only drawing attention to the fact that it would require so many trains and so many railroads to handle even one hundred million bushels of grain, which was the crop of last year. Now, with the influx of population to that country which has been taking place lately, what will it) be two or three years hence when you have four hundred million bushels of grain ? Why, even twelve or fifteen railroads could not handle it. Therefore it will be apparent how impossible it is to get sufficient accommodation to handle the crop of that country in the short time the farmers think it ought to be handled. Then if you had the roads, what would they be doing for the other nine months of the year ? They would not have the freight to haul, their earning powers would be nil, the irons would be rusting, there would be no interest earned on their money. Therefore that is not a solution of the difficulty. What the North-west farmer wants is to handle that crop in the fall of the year.

The hon. gentleman says there will be no use for these railways the rest of the year after taking out the grain. Have we not endeavoured to show this fact, that the present railway facilities are not able to cope with the commercial business of the country going westward ? There is not the slightest danger of the road running out of work the whole year.

I admit that there is a great deal more work offering for the railways than can be done, but I am starting from the desire of the farmer to move his crop in a short time, and I say that it would require twelve or fifteen roads to move in that short time the grain that is likely to offer in a very few years hence. But it would not require that number of railways to haul freight into the country, therefore some of them would be lying idle a good portion of the year. It seems to me that the only solution of this question is by building a road to the Hudson Bay. I travelled through that country for several weeks last fall, and endeavoured to get as much information about it as I could, and I frankly confess that I think this is the only solution of the situation. You are as near Hudson Bay from Regina, or Brandon, or perhaps Winnipeg, as you are to Port Arthur.
How long would the season of navigation be ?

From all the information I can get, I think there is navigation on the



Hudson Bay about four or five mouths in the year, or a little longer.
At what date would it close in the fall ?
The best navigation of the Hudson Bay Company 'commences some time in July.
And what is the probable date that bay navigation would close ?

I did not get any specific date, but my opinion is that there is between five and six months . of navigation, say at least four months. It commences towards the end of July, and you have August, September, October and November.
We can use the lakes up to the end of the first week in December. So by shipping to the bay we could not have any longer season.

But you have this advantage, that when you reach Hudson Bay you reach ocean navigation, where you can never have a blockade, because if you have freight offering, there will always be vessels to carry it away. You will not do as you do at Port Arthur, fill your elevators in a few weeks. When you come to an ocean port you cannot have a blockade. Then you have a great reduction in the cost of transportation.
I should think there would be a blockade during the six, or seven, or eight months that the hon. gentleman says navigation may be closed.

I say if you must handle the grain as the farmers desire it should be handled, inside of two or three months, that is the only feasible scheme for handling it. At best you have only to haul it four or five hundred miles. You can easily run several roads to the bay, as it is a cheap country to build through. If the great object to be attained is to haul the grain to the seaboard in a short time, I say that is the only way it can be done. But there are other ways of disposing of this trade.
Now, I notice that there is an important trade springing up with China and Japan. A great deal of the grain grown in the west is made into flour and shipped to the Orient, China and Japan, and will go in increasing quantities in the future. Then another portion of it will be consumed in the east. A large and increasing portion of it will be fed to stock, as is now being done in the older provinces. Take the province of Ontario. There are five to ten times as much grain, including wheat, oats, barley and pease, now fed to stock as was fed ten or fifteen years ago. And so it will be in the west if the farmers turn their attention to mixed farming. They will not have such a large quantity of grain to ship out of that country because it will be used up in the country in making another product that will be more easily taken Mr. SPROULE.
out and the movement of which can be distributed over a longer season. These are some of the difficulties that a farmer has to contend with there, and if be insists that the government must provide railways in the immediate future to handle that great crop in a short time he is proposing something that no government can accomplish no matter how much money is spent. That is my opinion in regard to it and my opinion as to the solution of the difficulty. I think what I have suggested is the only feasible solution in sight. There are those who say that the Hudson's Bay is not navigable. Well, I am not going to waste the time of the House to argue that question. At least I am satisfied from what information I have been able to get that it is navigable and navigable between four and five months in the year, hut if there is any question as to it, why do the government delay one hour from making a proper test? Why don't they send up one, or five, or even ten expeditions if necessary to collect data, from year to year to determine whether it is navigable or not and do that right away ? Why do they delay ? Because I have no doubt this will become at some time in the future one of the great highways of commerce for the people of that country. As one of the people living in the east I say it is not the desire of eastern people to be niggardly in expenditure to help the farmers of the west. They have been giving every attention to this subject and are just as anxious as their friends in the west that some solution should be found for the difficulties of life which they have to contend with. But they should remember that there are insurmountable difficulties that cannot be always overcome and that it is not only in the west that cars cannot be supplied when they are required.

As the general desire to discuss this question has prevailed I think at this late hour with the pea-mission of the House I shall ask leave to withdraw the motion for Supply and move that this House at the next sitting shall resolve itself into Committee of Supply.

The question is upon the motion of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Earle) that the House do now adjourn. Is it the pleasure of the House that the hon. gentleman has leave to withdraw his motion.
Motion withdrawn.
That the House resolve itself into Committee of Supply at the next sitting of the House.
What position will that put this side of the House in in regard to the moving of an amendment. If the motion of the hon. Minister of Finance passes now we will not be able to move an amendment.

No, the ordinary motion will stand. It is in order that we may retain the motion for Supply in the usual position, that I make this motion. There will be no change and the usual motion will have to be made.

Motion agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the business taken up to-morrow, and if the government Bills are to be taken up will the hon. miu-inster tell us which ?

We will take up, first, to-morrow, the Bill of the Postmaster General (Sir William. Mulock), item sixteen on the Order Paper for to-day, Bill (No. 17) to aid in the settlement of railway labour disputes, to be followed by item seventeen, Bill (No. 21) to amend and consolidate the law respecting railways if there be time, although the first item may occupy some time.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.25 a.m., Wednesday.
